#10536. 9 Cyber Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Maze of Threats

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

Practical guidance on safer search, stronger login security, better executive protection, and other habits can reduce enterprise risk.

9 Cybersecurity Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Threats

Cybersecurity Awareness Month tends to bring no shortage of advice, but the most useful guidance for business readers is the kind that maps to the way attacks actually happen now: through everyday habits, trusted workflows, and small moments of inattention. Risks show up when employees trust a search result, follow a fake CAPTCHA prompt, scan a login QR code, click a social ad, reuse a weak recovery method, or assume that an artificial intelligence (AI) model, executive device, or home network is secure by default. This article, compiled by the Dark Reading staff, and the accompanying videos bring those risks together in one place and focus on the practical behaviors and controls that can reduce them.

In October, a Dark Reading poll asked site visitors, "What's your biggest Cybersecurity Awareness Month challenge?" Readers identified phishing and social engineering as the top risk (39.1% of respondents), but that was neck-and-neck with shadow AI and risky data sharing (38.2%). A distant third was training fatigue and weak follow-through, identified as the top problem by 13.5% of respondents, and third-party and contractor access, with 9.2% of the vote.

Reader responses when asked, "What's your biggest Cybersecurity Awareness Month challenge?" Source: Dark Reading

The following nine tips can move the dial on that enterprise risk in very real ways. A common thread for all of these is the fact that attackers win by abusing convenience, familiarity, and human trust, whether the issue is SEO poisoning, ClickFix, session hijacking, dark patterns, or dodgy ads on Facebook. That's why awareness training still matters. It shouldn't be a once-a-year affair either, but rather an everyday focus on a set of specific, repeatable habits backed by stronger enterprise safeguards.

For security leaders, Cybersecurity Awareness Month gives them the chance to do more than remind users to "be careful." It is an opportunity to push for better defaults: phishing-resistant multifactor authentication (MFA), tighter privilege controls, better reporting paths, safer browsing habits, stronger executive protection, and more realistic guidance for work that happens outside the office. The goal is to make the safe action the default action and to help employees recognize the red flags before a routine click becomes a business problem.

Embrace cybersecurity awareness in October and beyond with Dark Reading's curated hub for security leaders — featuring expert news, analysis, and insights for hardening enterprise defenses in areas like identity security, AI risk, social engineering, supply chain, and more.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Becky Bracken, Media & Projects Director at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

As enterprises look to embrace agentic AI, they're sorting through frontier models, open-weight alternatives, and overseas offerings. Much of the focus is on evaluating the safeguards that, say, Claude might have vs. an open-weight alternative, like Meta's Llama series. But for business leaders, the key question is not which model is inherently safe; it's whether your organization has put adequate controls around it. That means treating AI just like any other high-impact enterprise system that can be misconfigured, manipulated, abused, or compromised.

Every model type comes with trade-offs. Frontier models may offer stronger vendor tooling, safety features, and governance support, but they can also introduce concentration and third-party risk. Open-weight models can give enterprises more transparency and control, but that control comes with more responsibility for hardening, patching, monitoring, and misuse prevention. Either way, the burden is on the enterprise.

For Cybersecurity Awareness Month, the practical takeaway is to assume compromise and build from there. Security teams should treat model weights, code, training data, prompts, plug-ins, APIs, and downstream applications as one attack surface. Limit what models can access. Restrict permissions. Segment AI workloads from critical systems. Log activity aggressively. Test for prompt injection, data leakage, and identity abuse. And keep humans in the loop for consequential actions, especially when money, customer data, or operational decisions are involved.

This is a golden opportunity for cybersecurity teams to become business enablers in the best sense of the term. AI will move fast, vendors will keep promising better safeguards, and the market will keep generating noise. But the durable security advantage will come from steady internal discipline. AI models can help the business, but they cannot be trusted to protect the business.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Alex Culafi, Senior News Writer at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

ClickFix is a simple but effective attack because it exploits something security teams deal with every day: people trying to solve a problem quickly. The user lands on a compromised or malicious Web site, a phishing page, or a fake browser-based meeting screen and sees what looks like a normal verification or troubleshooting prompt.

But instead of asking them to check a box, the page tells them to open a system tool — often with Windows + R — and paste in a command that the site has already copied to their clipboard. Once they do, they can trigger the compromise themselves. Security researchers note that this technique has risen sharply and often relies on fake CAPTCHA or error messages that make the request seem routine.

No legitimate CAPTCHA, website, or meeting platform should ever ask a user to open Run, PowerShell, Terminal, or Command Prompt and paste in a script. A request like that should be treated as an immediate red flag. The attack works precisely because it looks like a harmless fix and can sidestep some browser-based protections by pushing the user to execute the command themselves.

Organizations should build this into awareness training now. Tell employees to stop immediately if a website asks them to copy and paste commands, press unusual key combinations, or "fix" an issue through a local system tool. Reinforce a simple rule: If a prompt moves from the browser into the operating system, assume it's suspicious until IT says otherwise. Also, make it easy to report these incidents fast because early notification can help security teams contain the damage and identify affected users quickly. Restricting access to system tools where appropriate can add another layer of defense.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Rob Wright, Senior News Director at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

For Cybersecurity Awareness Month, here's a useful reminder for business leaders and employees alike: Treat social media ads as untrusted content. According to Gen Digital research, nearly one in three (31%) ads on Instagram and Facebook lead to scams, phishing pages, or malware.

And according to Reuters, Meta is charging higher premiums for advertisers that are considered risky. So not only have these platforms turned into a virtual minefield of scams, but Meta has a financial incentive to keep these ads online.

That matters because malicious ads often don't look malicious. They may mimic legitimate brands, use convincing creative, and point to spoofed URLs that appear credible at first glance. Even security-aware users can get caught. The real danger is that these ads exploit trust, urgency, and familiarity — exactly the tactics that work on busy professionals who are clicking quickly on personal devices outside the protections of corporate security tools.

The best defensive habit is simple: Do not click directly from social ads to make purchases, log in, or share payment information. If an offer looks legitimate, navigate to the brand's site manually, use a bookmarked link, or search for the company independently. Before entering credentials or card details, verify the domain carefully. Organizations should reinforce this behavior in security awareness training, especially for executives and remote workers who often blend personal and professional device use.

Caution remains the first line of defense. Encourage employees to use payment cards with fraud alerts, enable MFA on shopping and social accounts, and maintain healthy skepticism toward "limited-time" deals delivered through ad feeds.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Arielle Waldman, Features Writer at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

Ransomware has moved beyond encrypting systems and stealing data. Increasingly, attackers are pressuring organizations by targeting the people around their leaders: spouses, children, relatives, and close friends.

The "Semperis 2026 Ransomware Risk Report" found that 37% of attacks involved threats against employees' friends or family members. In other words, if attackers can't break your defenses fast enough, they may try to break your people instead. AI is accelerating this shift by making reconnaissance faster and cheaper, and threat actors can mine social media, public records, leaked data, and digital breadcrumbs to map relationships, impersonate trusted contacts, and build highly convincing social engineering campaigns.

For Cybersecurity Awareness Month, organizations should expand executive protection beyond the corporate perimeter. Start with digital footprint reduction: Encourage executives and family members to limit public exposure, remove unnecessary personal details from social profiles, and use aliases or less identifiable display names where practical. Establish family verification procedures, including safe words or challenge-response phrases, but rotate them regularly because any phrase used in a compromised channel should be treated as burned.

Most importantly, extend basic cyber hygiene to the household. Require strong unique passwords, enforce MFA on personal and shared accounts, secure home networks and connected devices, and train family members to recognize urgency-based scams, impersonation attempts, and suspicious content. A child's gaming console, a spouse's reused password, or a relative's overshared profile can become the opening attackers need.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Fahmida Rashid, Editor-in-Chief at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

Security awareness works better when it feels practical and relevant, not like a mandatory lecture. But one lesson is worth stating plainly: Some employees need more protection simply because they hold more power, more access, and more sensitive information. That starts with the C-suite, but it also applies to executive assistants, finance leaders, admins, and anyone else with privileged access.

Executives are high-value targets because they combine authority, visibility, and convenience-driven work habits. They approve payments, access sensitive strategy, and often log in from airports, hotels, and personal devices. That makes them especially attractive for phishing, impersonation, business email compromise, deepfake scams, and data theft. The right response is not to make life easier for them. It's to add smart friction in the places that matter most.

A strong executive protection program should include:

Phishing-resistant MFA, ideally hardware-based rather than SMS codes

Just-in-time privileged access instead of standing elevated permissions

Dedicated, locked-down devices for sensitive work

Stronger email and DLP controls to catch unusual forwarding, sharing, or exfiltration patterns

Focused coaching for executives and their inner circle, including assistants and chiefs of staff

Guidance for family and home networks because executive risk doesn't stop at the office

Organizations can focus on "white-glove" security, which means tighter controls, better support, and faster escalation when something looks off. If a control feels mildly annoying, that may be a sign it is doing its job.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Arielle Waldman, Features Writer at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

These design tricks train people to click quickly, surrender data reflexively, and ignore warning signs. Over time, that weakens judgment. Employees who get used to manipulative prompts may be less likely to notice when a request is truly malicious — whether that's a fake consent banner, a spoofed login page, a bogus app permission screen, or a prompt asking for sensitive information. Dark patterns blur the line between annoying and dangerous.

Another good rule: If you didn't sign up for a tool, don't create an account just because an email nudges you to. Unapproved sign-ups can create shadow accounts that IT and security teams can't monitor or secure.

Finally, build a reporting culture around anything that feels off — surprise charges, mystery accounts, unusual permissions, or suspicious prompts. The more comfortable employees are raising small concerns, the easier it is to catch bigger issues before they spread.

Everyone knows password hygiene remains a challenge for most businesses, but risk in the login journey increasingly extends to the other seams around identity — the moments where users, devices, sessions, and recovery workflows intersect.

The threats include quishing, where a user scans a QR code from an email, Web page, or physical sign and lands on a convincing but malicious login screen. There's also push fatigue, where attackers bombard a user with approval requests until one gets accepted. And it includes session hijacking and token theft, where the attacker skips the password entirely and hops into an already authenticated session. Add SIM swapping to intercept SMS-based recovery, and the modern login chain starts to look brittle in several different places.

The long-term fix is to move toward phishing-resistant authentication, including FIDO2 security keys and passkeys, backed by enterprise controls that verify context, not just credentials. That requires checking device posture, monitoring session behavior, requiring managed devices for sensitive systems, and reauthenticating when risk changes. In short: Don't just trust the login — trust the device, the session, and the user behavior behind it.

However, if this kind of full passkey rollout is not on the docket yet, here are some practical steps organizations can take now to reduce login risk:

Turn on number matching for push-based MFA

Reduce or eliminate SMS-based authentication where possible

Shorten session lifetimes for high-risk apps

Require managed-device access for sensitive systems

Trigger reauthentication when device posture changes

Meanwhile, employee training should focus on a few clear habits: Don't scan login QR codes from unsolicited messages or unverified sources, for one, and never approve an unexpected SMS verification push.

To prevent session hijacking, log out of accounts when you finish using them, rather than just closing the browser tab. And avoid public Wi-Fi when you're doing something sensitive.

Finally, on the SIM-swapping front, switch from SMS MFA to Authenticator Apps that can't be intercepted via a phone network. You can also request that account changes require physical ID in-store or multilayered, out-of-band authentication before processing SIM changes.

Account takeover attacks are a bugbear that is unlikely to disappear anytime soon, but increasing friction and cost for attackers throughout the login process can truly help and, hopefully at the very least, get you out of the low-hanging-fruit category.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Rob Wright, Senior News Director at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

Fall youth sports season means many parent-professionals are working from the sidelines — at soccer fields, hockey rinks, football stadiums, and school gyms — often on whatever free Wi-Fi happens to be available. That may not sound as risky as logging on at a major airport or hotel, but it still creates an opportunity for mistakes that attackers, pranksters, or opportunistic snoops can exploit.

So, although sophisticated nation-state actors are probably not camping out at your local rink, there's still considerable risk if you connect to the wrong network. A hotspot with a name that closely resembles the venue's legitimate Wi-Fi can be enough to trick a busy parent checking email between periods or joining a meeting from the bleachers. Even a spoofed network set up as a joke can expose traffic, credentials, or session data if employees are careless.

Business readers that want to avoid their employer's penalty box should treat public connectivity anywhere as untrusted by default. Before joining a network, verify the exact Wi-Fi name with venue staff or posted signage. Disable auto-join so your device does not connect to similarly named networks without your knowledge. Use only approved secure remote access tools, keep endpoint protections enabled, and avoid handling sensitive work, such as admin access, financial approvals, or password resets, over public Wi-Fi unless it is absolutely necessary.

If you need connectivity, a personal hotspot is often the safer option — but only if it is configured properly. Use a strong password, change the default network name if it reveals your identity, and make sure the hotspot is not left open to nearby devices.

The broader lesson for Cybersecurity Awareness Month: Low-profile locations can still produce real security failures. The setting may feel routine, but the network risk is not.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Alex Culafi, Senior News Writer at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

SEO poisoning turns a routine Google search into an attack path. Threat actors either build lookalike websites or compromise legitimate ones, then manipulate content and code so those pages rank highly in search results. The idea is that a user searching for software, a login page, or a partner site might simply click the top result, which happens to be poisoned, and subsequently hand over credentials or download malware.

Guidance on spotting fake websites specifically warns that SEO poisoning can push malicious sites to the top of search results, and Trend Micro's 2026 research on more than 35,000 fake World Cup-related sites shows how easily attackers can industrialize fake-site campaigns around high-interest topics.

For business users, the safest habit is to stop trusting search rankings as a signal of legitimacy. Before clicking, inspect the URL for misspellings, extra words, odd country codes, or brand names that look slightly off. After clicking, be suspicious if the page immediately pushes a download, asks for credentials too early, triggers repeated redirects, throws pop-ups, or trips a browser warning. Those are strong signs that something is wrong.

Organizations should reinforce a few simple rules in awareness training:

Use bookmarks or manually typed URLs for key business apps, vendors, and partner portals.

Verify domains before downloading software or entering credentials.

Treat urgent install prompts and so-called ClickFix instructions as red flags.

Report suspicious search results, spoofed pages, and accidental downloads to IT immediately.

Isolate the device and change credentials quickly if a user may have interacted with a fake site.

The practical message for Cybersecurity Awareness Month: Search is a convenience layer, not a trust layer. Employees don't need to become threat hunters, but they do need to slow down long enough to verify where a search result is actually taking them. That pause can prevent a compromise.

#10535. A Practical Introduction to the Twitch Helix API

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Behind almost every Twitch tool you have ever seen, the stat trackers, the moderation bots, the stream overlays, the alert systems, sits one interface: the Twitch Helix API. Twitch is unusually generous with public data, and Helix is the door to it. If you have ever wondered how third-party sites know who is live, what a channel's viewership looks like, or details a Twitch profile page does not even display, this is the machinery.

This article is a practical overview of Helix for developers who have not used it yet: what it offers, how its authentication works, what people build with it, and where the sharp edges are.

Helix is Twitch's current REST API, served from api.twitch.tv/helix. It replaced the old "Kraken" API, which was fully retired in 2022, so any tutorial still showing Kraken endpoints is a sign to keep scrolling. Helix covers users, streams, channels, games and categories, clips, chat, moderation actions, subscriptions, and events, with JSON in and JSON out.

Two things distinguish it from many platform APIs. First, a large share of it works without any user's permission, because the data is public by Twitch's own definition. Second, it is paired with EventSub, a push system that notifies your application when things happen (a stream goes live, a user follows, a message arrives) instead of forcing you to poll. Most serious Twitch tools use both: Helix for lookups, EventSub for live events.

Authentication is where most newcomers stall, mainly because Twitch offers several OAuth flows and tutorials rarely say which one you actually need. The short version:

Every request needs a Client ID, which you get by registering an application in the Twitch developer console (two-factor authentication on your account is required first). Requests carry the Client ID and a bearer token together; forgetting the Client ID header is the classic mystery 401.

App access tokens come from the client credentials flow, a single server-to-server request with your ID and secret. They have no user attached and that is fine, because public reads, user profiles, live streams, top games, clips, need no user context. For most read-only tools, this is the only flow you ever touch.

Tokens expire, so real applications cache them with their reported lifetime and refresh on a 401 rather than assuming a token lives forever.

A tour of the endpoints that power most tools:

Users. Give the users endpoint a username and it returns the account's public record: display name, profile image, description, Affiliate or Partner status, and the account's exact creation timestamp. That last field is interesting because Twitch does not display it anywhere on a profile, yet it is one of the platform's most useful trust signals, moderators use account age to spot throwaway accounts, and streamers use it to filter giveaway entries. The creation date alone powers a small subcategory of tools: free account age checkers, such as Twitch account age checker, are essentially this one endpoint with a clean page around it, taking any public username and returning the creation date, age, avatar, and broadcaster status. It is a good illustration of how far a single well-chosen Helix field can go.

Streams. The stream's endpoint reports who is live right now, with titles, categories, thumbnail URLs, and viewer counts. This is the backbone of every "is my favorite streamer live" notifier and every directory-style site, and polling it over time is how stat trackers chart viewership history.

Games and categories. Top games, category search, and metadata. Combined with streams data, this is how analytics sites rank categories and how tools answer "how crowded is this category right now."

Clips and videos. Clip metadata, view counts, and creation tools. Highlight compilers and clip-sharing bots live here.

Helix enforces a points-based rate limit per Client ID, and every response tells you where you stand through Ratelimit-Limit, Ratelimit-Remaining, and Ratelimit-Reset headers. Well-behaved tools read those headers and back off before hitting zero; badly behaved ones retry 429s in a loop and wonder why things get worse. For lookup-style tools the practical fix is caching, data like account creation dates never changes, so there is no reason to ask twice.

A few more edges worth knowing before they bite:

Usernames change, IDs do not. Store user IDs, not logins, or your saved data will eventually point at the wrong person.

Missing users are not errors. Looking up a nonexistent username returns a successful response with an empty data array, so handle the empty case explicitly.

Batching exists. The users endpoint takes up to 100 logins in one call, which matters the moment your tool checks lists instead of individuals.

Secrets stay server-side. The client secret identifies your application; calling the token endpoint from browser code hands your app's identity to anyone who opens devtools. Public-facing tools put a small server between the browser and Twitch.

The reason Twitch's third-party ecosystem is so large is that the barrier is so low: one public API, generous free access, and a platform where small questions genuinely matter to people. That is why the space is full of narrow tools that each answer one thing well, when was this account created, is this channel live, how fast is this category growing, which clips popped this week. Most of them are a weekend of work on top of one or two endpoints, and some of them grow into real products.

If you want to start, the path is short: register an application at the developer console, request an app access token, and call the users or streams endpoint for something you actually care about. The official documentation at dev.twitch.tv is current and well maintained, which is not something every platform can claim. Pick one piece of data Twitch collects but does not display, put a clean interface on it, and you are following the same recipe as most of the Twitch tools you already use.

#10533. Google Gemini rolling out ‘Memory summary’ with everything it remembers about you

Google Gemini now offers a “Memory summary” to “view, edit, and delete what Gemini Apps understands about you.”

On the web, you can access this new experience from Settings > Personal Intelligence (or gemini.google.com/personalization-settings).

This loads a list with categories like: The Essentials (“snapshot of your core background, location, and key relationships”), Career & Professional Projects, Travel & Daily Gear, Media & Entertainment, and Fitness & Lifestyle. Each has several bullet points with specific details.

The text field at the bottom lets you “Add or remove details.” For example:

Google says “Gemini may ask follow-up questions if your request is ambiguous to ensure your summary remains accurate.”

The pencil icon in the top-right corner lets you make broader edits. In the three-dot overflow menu, you’ll find “Memory history” to see “when specific information was added or modified.”

#10532. Germany Busts 'Crime-as-a-Service' Investment Fraud Outfit

Authorities seized more than 100 servers and arrested seven as part of a crackdown on a fraud network spanning more than 50 countries.

You see an online advertisement promising quick returns from trading cryptocurrency, foreign currencies, and stocks. You give the "investment firm" your information, and an operator calls you and convinces you to transfer a small amount of money into a platform. You make early profits quickly, so you deposit increasingly large sums of money. But when you attempt to withdraw your earnings, the operator stalls for a while until finally cutting off contact.

This pattern is familiar to victims of investment fraud, a multinational criminal industry that relies on social engineering to convince would-be investors that they're about to make substantial gains before pulling the rug out from under them.

Europol today shared news of the disruption of one such operation, an investment fraud scheme with potential victims across more than 50 countries and a company allegedly supplying fraudulent trading platforms and leads to criminal groups. According to a press release, Europol and Eurojust supported an international operation involving authorities in Albania, Cyprus, Finland, Germany, Israel, Kosovo, and North Macedonia.

Related:Attackers in Binance Breach Targeted Known Weakness, Missing Controls

The German Itzehoe Public Prosecutor's Office led the operation, targeting a company suspected of supplying phony trading websites and multiple call centers to criminal groups; investigators estimate losses to exceed 4 million euros.

International authorities searched 17 locations, including a call center in Kosovo, leading to the seizure of 100 servers and the arrests of seven suspects.

The law enforcement action reflects a multiyear investigation that began in 2022, according to Europol, when a German couple reported they could not withdraw money invested through an online trading platform. This led to two previous "action days" by authorities, one in 2022 (involving two arrests and the seizure of evidence) and another in 2025 (involving more arrests and seizures of money and evidence).

"Analysis of the material recovered exposed the suspected infrastructure provider and its links to call centre operators, paving the way for the latest operation," the press release read.

A Eurojust press release provided further detail regarding the extent of the operation. The analysis of evidence seized during the second action day exposed a company based in Cyprus and Israel allegedly offering "crime-as-a-service," supplying criminal groups with fraudulent websites that funnel targets into the central investment scam.

The data of potential victims visiting these websites and expressing interest would be sold as leads to call centers, which contacted the victims to persuade them to invest their money, leading to repeated demands for additional investments. Authorities identified suspected call center-operating clients of this company in Albania, Kosovo, and North Macedonia.

Related:Getting Past the Post-Quantum Cryptography Discovery Phase

The fraud operation guaranteed significant returns for trades in cryptocurrencies, foreign currencies, or stocks, according to Europol. But authorities found that the seemingly legitimate platforms were run by "brokers" that used phony profits and social engineering tactics to convince victims to keep investing. Additionally, investigators also found the operators used affiliate marketing services and deceptive advertisements to lure in potential victims.

Austin Anderson, director of threat intel at cybercrime disruption firm Netcraft, tells Dark Reading that operations like these that target upstream providers can help disrupt investment fraud operations at scale.

"Fraudsters have increasingly specialized in one piece of an attack's supply chain, as seen in this scheme where websites collected personal data that was sold to call centers to ultimately coerce funds from victims," he says. "While this can breed sophistication in each actor's niche, it also introduces fragility when a large dependency like the call center is disrupted. Ultimately, without arrests that remove fraudsters from the market, these operations only temporarily disrupt operations while actors rebuild their infrastructure."

Related:Cyber Experts Weigh In: How to Fight Artex & AntiFox

#10530. Samsung bets that you’ll either buy a Galaxy S27 Pro or Ultra next year

Samsung is teeing up to kick off 2027 with an all-new lineup of flagship smartphones, and despite rising prices at your local Best Buy, the brand is still hedging that you’re going to pony up for the most premium model available.

As reported by ETNews, Samsung is currently allotting over 70 percent of its total production capabilities to just the Galaxy S27 Ultra and the new Galaxy S27 “Pro” model expected to launch alongside it. That leaves the plain Galaxy S27 and the larger S27+ on the outside looking in. In comparison to this year’s launch, the Galaxy S26 Ultra made up about 50 percent of this series’ production volume, for a grand total of 18 million units.

Historical performance implies Samsung is probably correct here. While big displays are typically what consumers are drawn to, it does appear that the S27 Pro won’t be all that much smaller than the S27+. Considering the Pro should slot in right around the typical price point as the Plus model, it’s not hard to imagine plenty of would-be S27+ buyers moving to the Pro.

For what it’s worth, Samsung betting big on high-end devices usually pays off. We’re on year two of the Fold series seeing big successes — first with the redesigned Fold 7 in 2025, then with the reshaped Fold 8 this year — and the Galaxy S26 Ultra managed to become the best-selling Android phone in Q2 of this year in a list typically populated by iPhones and cheap Galaxy A-series models. Even with prices constantly on the rise, the people yearn for flagship smartphones. You just have to wonder where that ceiling actually is.

#10526. Self-Hosted LangSmith Alternatives: 4 Tools Tested on One TypeScript Agent

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

LangSmith is closed-source and restricts self-hosting to enterprise licenses, teams that run their own LLMOps stack and want to keep traces on their own servers need an alternative. To find the best fit, we set a baseline by tracing a small TypeScript agent (equipped with two tools) in LangSmith Cloud. Then, we ran the exact same agent through Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, Opik, and AcruxCore using each platform's recommended TypeScript setup. All tests were run on November 5, 2026, and we pulled every trace back through each tool's API to verify the data.

All four alternatives successfully recreated LangSmith’s trace tree for the test prompt: a single agent span containing three LLM calls and two tool calls. The real differences between them come down to how much boilerplate code you have to write, how spans are typed, whether costs are tracked, and the overall server footprint.

Why Teams Look for a LangSmith Alternative

LangSmith remains the best choice if you already use LangChain and allow cloud hosting—it required just 25 lines of code in our test. The alternatives below are for teams that don't fit that profile.

To test these platforms, we built a simple customer support agent equipped with two tools:

Both tools use static fixture data to ensure every test run is identical. The agent runs a standard loop: it prompts the model, executes any requested tools, and stops once the model provides a final answer.

We tested the agent with three specific prompts to see how the tracing handled different levels of complexity:

For our comparison, we focused entirely on the third question because it generates a robust, multi-step trace.

Under the hood, the agent uses the standard openai package to call the qwen3.8-flash model. We originally picked this model based on its reliable tool-calling behavior during early probing thought it once skipped a tool call later.

We used LangSmith as our baseline. By tracing the agent there first, we created a checklist of every field it captured, and we judged all the alternatives against that exact list.

For setup, we followed the recommended TypeScript approach from each tool's documentation. Phoenix didn't have specific instructions for using its register() helper with OpenAI in TypeScript, so we adapted the pattern from their Anthropic guide.

Here is the agent with no tracing. Each tool section adds one tracing file that imports these files and changes nothing in them.

LangSmith traces the plain openai package with two helpers. wrapOpenAI records each model call, and traceable records your own functions. Without traceable on the run and the tools, wrapOpenAI alone gave three separate root runs and no tool runs.

This file adds 25 lines and removes 3, and installs one package.

LangSmith showed one root run with five children in call order: LLM, get_order_status, LLM, get_refund_policy, LLM. Every field it recorded became a row of the checklist table under "Results". Cost appeared only after a custom price entry. In our error run the failing tool was marked as an error, but the root stayed success: traceable turned the throw into a rejected promise that our agent did not await, so the agent carried on and answered.

Langfuse self-hosts as six containers, including ClickHouse, a column store built for large scans. In our measurement the stack held 2.60–2.64 GiB of memory at idle. Its Docker Compose guide recommends at least 4 CPU cores and 16 GiB RAM, with about 100 GiB of disk.

The TypeScript path is built on OpenTelemetry. You start the OTel Node SDK with LangfuseSpanProcessor, wrap the client with observeOpenAI, and wrap your own functions with observe:

This file adds 31 lines and removes 5, and installs four packages. We pinned the OTel Node SDK to 0.223.0, because @langfuse/otel 6.1.1 does not accept 0.300.0.

Langfuse successfully recreated the same trace tree, neatly tagging the spans as AGENT, GENERATION, and TOOL. It captured all the essentials: tool calls, tool definitions, and the complete message history. However, for the LLM output, it only saved the assistant's message—dropping the finish_reason, response ID, and the provider name.

We ran our deployment in Langfuse v4's events_only mode, which turns off the v1 trace endpoint. Because of this, the API didn't return a centralized trace object or root-level sums for tokens and costs, even though the UI calculated and displayed them perfectly (we didn't test other modes).

Costs showed up exactly as expected once we added a custom price entry. Since Langfuse calculates prices based on the specific usage types you define, and we only set rates for input and output, the separate reasoning tokens went unpriced. Finally, during our error test, the observe wrapper let the error bubble up to the agent, correctly flagging both the tool and the root span as an ERROR.

Phoenix self-hosts as two containers, one Python server and Postgres. In our measurement it held 0.47 GiB at idle. Phoenix is source-available under the Elastic License 2.0, so it is not open source. Authentication is off until you turn it on.

The TypeScript path uses Phoenix's register() helper and the OpenInference instrumentation for the OpenAI package. OpenInference is a set of OpenTelemetry attribute names for LLM spans. traceAgent and traceTool wrap the run and the tools:

This file adds 32 lines and removes 3, and installs three packages.

Phoenix rebuilt the same tree, typed as AGENT, LLM and TOOL. Each LLM span keeps the full OpenAI response object, plus the messages as flattened attributes. The root span stores no token count, but Phoenix computes a sum for the root and the trace when you read it. Cost and those sums are only in the GraphQL API and the UI, and the REST API has no per-trace endpoint.

Cost appeared after a custom price entry under Settings > Models, and Phoenix priced the reasoning tokens by falling back to the output price. In the error run, the tool span and the root were marked ERROR, and the tool span carried an exception event with the stack trace.

Opik self-hosts as eight containers, including ClickHouse, MySQL and ZooKeeper. In our measurement it held 3.69 GiB at idle, the most of the four. The self-hosted UI opened without a login, so every trace was readable from any machine that could reach the port.

The TypeScript path wraps the client with trackOpenAI and your own functions with track. By default trackOpenAI starts a new trace for every model call, so the file passes the run's span through the documented parent option:

This file adds 33 lines and removes 5. It installs opik-openai 2.2.142, and npm adds opik 1.11.14 as its peer, because opik-openai asks for opik ^1.8.61.

Opik successfully recreated the trace tree, and its trace object neatly tallies token counts across all LLM spans. In the logs, tool arguments are bundled into an array, and the LLM output only retains the assistant's message.

We did notice a quirk with the documented OpenAI wrapper (tested on the npm package opik 1.11.14): it tags model calls as general rather than llm, which incorrectly leaves the llm_span_count at zero. (We didn't test newer Opik core versions to see if this has changed). Additionally, because our synchronous tools execute in under a millisecond, they log the exact same start time as the subsequent LLM call, causing the UI to list the LLM call first out of order.

Cost tracking is entirely manual. Opik showed no costs by default, and the documentation doesn't mention a custom price table. We checked the configuration tabs on our 2.2.52 instance (Feedback definitions, AI Providers, Workspace preferences) and found no model pricing settings. To see costs, you have to manually assign a price to each individual span yourself—only the spans we hardcoded this way displayed a cost.

Finally, error reporting is highly detailed. If something fails, Opik attaches an error_info block—complete with the error type, message, and full traceback—directly to the tool span, the root span, and the overall trace.

AcruxCore self-hosts as five containers: Postgres, Redis, a Node API and worker, and nginx. In our measurement it held 0.39 GiB at idle, the least of the four. Its quickstart leaves sign-up open and ships a committed default GATEWAY_ENCRYPTION_KEY, which encrypts stored provider keys; replace it. We tested a local build from 2026-09-17.

The TypeScript path AcruxCore's docs put first is its gateway. The official openai client keeps working: you point its baseURL at ACRUXCORE_BASE_URL + "/gateway" and call a model registered in AcruxCore, which forwards each call to an OpenAI-compatible provider. The gateway records every model call as an llm span. The SDK's step helpers add the rest: traces.step opens the agent span, traces.wrap wraps each tool, and two headers file the gateway's spans under the agent span:

This file adds 30 lines and removes 5, and installs one package. It builds its own client, so it does not use provider.ts. The gateway refused our team API key, so the client uses a gateway virtual key created in the dashboard.

On this path every model call passes through the AcruxCore server, which none of the other four tools need. If you do not want a proxy in the request path, the SDK's register() helper sends OpenTelemetry spans from your process instead. On that path the step helpers do not join the openai package's spans, so you write the agent and tool spans by hand.

AcruxCore rebuilt the same tree, typed as agent, llm and tool, in call order. Each LLM span keeps the full response, the provider and the cached-token count, and the trace carries a token total. The LLM spans do not keep the tool definitions sent to the model, and no reasoning-token count was recorded. The trace took its name from the question, not from the agent span, and each LLM span is named by its start time.

Cost appeared on every LLM span and as a sum on the trace, from the custom price we set on the model in AcruxCore's model list. In the error run, the step helpers marked the tool span and the agent root as error with the error message, with no status code of ours. The API returned no stack trace.

All five tools accept traces over OTLP, the OpenTelemetry wire format. trace-otel.ts sends the same spans with no vendor package: the OTel Node SDK, the OTLP/HTTP protobuf exporter and the OpenInference OpenAI instrumentation. The exporter reads its endpoint and headers from environment variables:

We ran the two-tool question once per backend and changed only environment variables: the endpoint, the headers, and for Phoenix a resource attribute that sets the project name (without it, spans go to a default project). "Accepted" means the exporter reported success, which it does only for an HTTP 2xx, and we read the spans back through each API.

Opik stored the root and tool spans as general although AGENT and TOOL kinds were sent; the cause is Not tested. LangSmith mapped AGENT to its chain type. If you instrument with plain OTel and OpenInference attributes, your raw spans are not tied to one vendor, but span types, cost and trace views still differ by backend.

The first table covers setup: how much server each tool needs, how much code we changed in the agent, and how cost and the plain OTel exporter worked. Phoenix and AcruxCore had the smallest servers, and AcruxCore needed the fewest lines among the self-hosted tools. Opik was the only one without a price table.

The second table checks each trace against what LangSmith recorded for the same run, one field at a time. All five rebuilt the same tree with tokens and durations. They differ in span types, how much of the LLM output they keep, where token sums live, and how much detail they store for the failing tool.

Token totals for the two-tool question ranged from 1,910 to 2,111. Each tool traced a separate run and reasoning length varies, so these numbers do not compare the tools.

All five tools successfully traced our test agent, so the right choice really comes down to your team's specific constraints, infrastructure preferences, and how tracing fits into the rest of your MLOps tooling.

All four alternatives successfully recreated LangSmith’s trace tree. The real deciding factors are boilerplate code, span typing, cost tracking, and server bloat.

LangSmith remains the simplest option for LangChain users who can utilize the cloud. Otherwise, your choice depends on your priorities: Langfuse for community size, Phoenix for a lightweight Postgres footprint, Opik for strict Apache-2.0 compliance with deep error logging, or AcruxCore for combined tracing and tool governance on minimal hardware. Best of all, if you stick to standard OpenTelemetry spans, you aren't locked in—you can try them all and easily pivot later.

#10525. Whipped cream sold at Costco is being recalled because it could have cleaning chemicals inside

Thanksgiving is less than two weeks away, which means millions of Americans will soon be sitting down to pumpkin and pecan pies topped with healthy doses of whipped cream.

But now a popular whipped cream product sold at Costco is being recalled over fears that it could be contaminated with cleaning chemicals. Here’s what you need to know.

What happened?

Discount wholesale giant Costco announced a recall of one of its whipped cream products sold under the company’s Kirkland Signature brand. The alert was posted on Costco’s recalls website with a November 7 notice from Alamance Foods.

Alamance Foods specializes in manufacturing dairy creams and foams as well as beverages and other products for retailers and grocery chains’ private-label brands.

For Costco, Alamance Foods manufactures select Kirkland Signature Whipped Cream products.

The recall is voluntary, the notice states, and is being done “out of an abundance of caution” after it was found that the product “may contain a small amount of a cleaning chemical.”

What Kirkland Signature Whipped Cream product is being recalled?

According to the recall notice, one type of Kirkland Signature Whipped Cream product is being recalled:

  • Product: Kirkland Signature Real Heavy Whipped Cream, 15 oz (425 g), case pack 8CT/3PK, item code AC50
  • Lot: 04/02/2027 (Best If Used By APR/02/27)
  • Timestamps affected on can: 00:35 – 02:45

Images of the recalled product’s packaging are available in the recall notice here.

Where was the recalled product sold?

According to the notice, the recalled whipped cream product was sold in the following states:

  • Alabama
  • Florida
  • Georgia
  • Iowa
  • Illinois
  • Indiana
  • Missouri
  • Mississippi
  • North Carolina
  • South Carolina
  • Tennessee
  • Wisconsin

Has anyone been harmed by the recalled whipped cream?

Thankfully, there are no reports of illness or other harm to consumers who have purchased the now-recalled whipped cream. 

“Members have reported a chemical smell and taste, but no serious adverse effects requiring medical care have been reported,” the November 7 recall notice states.

What should I do if I have the recalled whipped cream?

Do not consume it. Instead, the recall notice states you should stop using it and instead return the item to Costco for a full refund.

Consumers with questions about the recall can contact Alamance Foods at customer.care@alamancefood.com.

#10522. Pharmaceutical ads may influence which drug AI recommends, new research finds

Next time you ask AI for medical advice, you may want to consider whether it’s been influenced by Big Pharma. Prescription drug advertisements are everywhere and may affect AI’s recommendations, according to a study published in The Lancet Digital Health this week.

The study authors conducted experiments with a dozen consumer-facing large language models (LLMs), including versions of Claude, Gemini, and ChatGPT—made by Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI, respectively. 

Clinical guidance or commercial influence?

The models were tested across 33 scenarios that each included a clinical case description and multiple treatment options. In some cases, the AI models were also given an ad for one of the treatment options. The ad’s content included information about the drug and its uses, but did not specifically direct the AI model to recommend the drug.

When exposed to an ad, AI models recommended the treatment in question an average of 47.6% of the time, compared with 35% when no ad was present. However, the size of these shifts varied among the 12 models.

Although the models often changed their recommendation when an ad was present, in most cases they still selected one of the appropriate options. The outputs only disclosed the ad’s presence about 30% of the time. 

“An answer can be clinically reasonable and still raise an important question about why the AI arrived at that answer,” study author Dr. Girish Nadkarni, a professor of medicine and system chair of the Windreich Department of Artificial Intelligence and Human Health at Mount Sinai’s Icahn School of Medicine, said in a statement. “As AI becomes part of how people get health information, we need to be able to distinguish clinical guidance from commercial influence and be transparent about when advertising is part of the interaction.”

Pharmaceutical companies spent more than $6 billion on TV advertising alone in 2024, according to a report by the pharmaceutical data, analytics, and consulting firm IQVIA, which said that direct-to-consumer advertising “directly influences patient requests and prescription rates, driving real action in healthcare.”

Most countries ban drug ads

All high-income countries, save for the U.S. and New Zealand, ban direct-to-consumer ads for prescription drugs.

In the U.S., prescription drugs consume more than 30% of commercial time during major networks’ evening news programs, according to a 2025 press release from the U.S. Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

Last year, ranking member Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the End Prescription Drug Ads Now Act, co-signed by six other senators, which would ban such advertising, including on social media. 

In practice, the Lancet study said, AI models could be exposed to drug ads “through user prompts, application-added context, retrieved online material, or inadvertent or malicious insertion,” and that, “unlike television or print advertising, which is subject to U.S. Food and Drug Administration oversight, AI-mediated promotion might not fit existing categories.” 

However, the study did not examine whether these measured effects translate into real-world changes in patient requests or prescriptions.

The chatbot will see you now

In a recent Doximity survey of 3,379 U.S. physicians, 54% said they had moderate or high levels of trust in AI’s ability to recommend treatment or management. Three-quarters of respondents also said patients had become more likely to propose a diagnosis or treatment plan suggested by AI over the past six months. 

“Clinicians might defer to algorithmic recommendations even when they conflict with clinical judgment,” the study’s authors said, and an appropriate but ad-influenced suggestion “might provide little reason to question it.”

#10520. The untapped potential of a smarter SPIFF strategy

Manufacturers invest a lot in getting their products into the right channels. But once those products reach a dealer network, the brand gives up a significant amount of control over what happens next.

Suddenly, someone outside your organization is responsible for understanding your products, remembering what differentiates them, and recommending them when the right customer walks through the door.

And they may be doing the same thing for dozens of competing brands.

That’s one reason sales performance incentive funds (SPIFFs) have become such a familiar tool. Give retail sales associates a financial incentive to sell a particular product, and you create an immediate reason to prioritize it.

But an incentive alone can only do so much. The bigger opportunity is using the SPIFF to engage dealers more consistently. It can help you build a strategy around the program that reinforces your brand remaining relevant long after the initial announcement.

THE INCENTIVE AS PART OF THE EXPERIENCE

It’s easy to think about a SPIFF primarily in terms of the offer: How much will participants earn? Which products qualify? How long will the promotion run? But also consider why someone would continue paying attention to the program. And consider the experience from the dealer’s perspective.

You’ll want to ensure the program is clearly explained and that registration is easy. Make it very obvious which products qualify and why they are worth recommending. Include a list of useful selling points to use while talking to customers. And ask yourself whether they are being reminded about the opportunity after the program launch.

A SPIFF can have an attractive incentive and still underperform if it isn’t reinforced after launch or the experience around it creates friction. The strongest programs address motivation and engagement.

PRODUCT EDUCATION

A financial reward gives someone a reason to make a sale, but product knowledge helps them make that sale confidently.

Retail sales associates often recommend products among multiple brands that can meet a customer’s needs. If your brand wants to earn the recommendation, the person making it needs to understand why your product is relevant to the customer standing in front of them.

Customers want to know what makes your product different. They’re looking for relevant benefits that matter to them along with proof points to back up the recommendation. And it helps to know which products are right for which customers.

A SPIFF creates a natural opportunity to reinforce those issues. Product education should be built into the communications surrounding it. Use the program to continually give dealers useful information they can apply on the sales floor.

Over time, that familiarity can build something even more valuable: brand preference. When sales associates understand your products and appreciate what makes them different, they will feel confident recommending them. They can become genuine advocates for your brand. And in a competitive retail environment, having an informed, enthusiastic advocate on the sales floor can be a powerful differentiator.

MAINTAIN THE PROGRAM AFTER LAUNCH

Many marketing initiatives receive their greatest communications push at the beginning. There’s the launch email. The sales materials. The landing page. Maybe a kickoff meeting or announcement. Then attention moves elsewhere.

The problem is that your dealers’ attention moves elsewhere, too. Sustained participation requires sustained visibility. You need to create a communications cadence that gives people reasons to keep paying attention.

Remind them about the opportunity and highlight featured products. Reinforce key selling points and share program updates. Give internal sales teams tools to continue the conversation. Use consumer-facing marketing to help create demand that supports what dealers are being asked to sell.

Each touchpoint can reinforce the others. That’s when a collection of promotional tactics starts becoming an integrated dealer engagement strategy.

THINK BEYOND THE SPIFF

The larger lesson extends beyond any single incentive program. Manufacturers that sell through dealers depend on people outside their organizations to represent their brands every day. Yet dealer engagement can easily become transactional. To combat this, communicate when there’s a new product or promotion, or something else the dealer can focus on.

There’s an opportunity to think more broadly.

The goal is to make your brand easier to understand, easier to sell, and easier to remember. That means giving dealers the information they need to better serve their customers. Manufacturers should ensure that sales and marketing efforts reinforce one another, and use it to consistently build familiarity and confidence that make your brand the one they genuinely prefer to recommend.

A SPIFF can provide an ideal moment to put those principles into practice. By making the experience more engaging, educational, and valuable for retail sales associates, manufacturers have an opportunity to build stronger brand relationships.

Manufacturers can potentially turn occasional sellers into enthusiastic brand ambassadors. Because when a sales associate has a genuine preference for your brand, that connection can influence recommendations long after the incentive ends.

Chris K. Bailey is president and CEO of Bailey Brand Consulting.

#10518. Hunter is killing Google Home, Alexa controls for its smart ceiling fans

Hunter, a major brand for ceiling fans in the US, is pulling the plug on its Google Home and Amazon Alexa bridge for controlling “HunterSMART” models in just a few weeks.

Effective January 1, 2027, Hunter will pull support for the cloud-reliant “HunterSMART” connection used for Google Home and Amazon Alexa controls. Hunter’s app and the included remote will continue to work, but connections to smart home ecosystems will not.

Beginning January 1, 2027, the legacy cloud-to-cloud connections used for app linking between the HunterSMART™ mobile apps and Google Home and/or Amazon Alexa will no longer be supported.

After this date, Google home and Alexa functionality that relies on this legacy cloud connection will no longer work for HunterSMART fans, including voice commands, scenes, and automations.

This bridge is going away in favor of a Matter connection, with Hunter having been upgrading select models to be Matter-compatible over the past year. But this is only available to “eligible” models, not everyone who was already using Hunter’s existing bridge. A list of compatible models is available on Hunter’s website, with firmware updates rolling out via the HunterSMART app.

Some models, such as the one I reviewed a few years ago, require updated hardware. Besides that, the one I have can’t even be re-connected to Wi-Fi to check for an update as Hunter’s Android app consistently crashes during the setup process.

Once the fan has been updated, it won’t be available via the existing link and will instead require re-pairing via your smart home app of choice, whether that’s Google Home or another.

…Hunter is transitioning eligible HunterSMART™ products to Matter, an industry standard designed to support broader smart-home compatibility.

If your fan is eligible for Matter-compatibility, you will be able to continue using all smart functionality within the Google Home and/or Alexa ecosystems after completing the applicable Matter migration & setup.

Once your HunterSMART fan is Matter-enabled, connecting your fan to Google and Alexa will work differently than it does today. Instead of linking your HunterSMART account to Google Home or Alexa, you will need to setup your Matter-enabled fan directly into these compatible ecosystems using the Matter setup available via the Google Home and/or Alexa apps. Matter-enabled devices do not use the legacy cloud linking service for smart controls that is being discontinued.

How can I migrate my HunterSMART fan to Matter?

Depending on your fan model and hardware configuration, a firmware update or updated hardware components may be required for Matter compatibility. Available Matter upgrade options and instructions will vary by product. You can visit our HunterSMART™ Matter resource page for the latest information about Matter compatibility, available upgrade options, and next steps.

#10517. OpenAI board member makes a terrifying prediction: You will probably die from an AI accident

Anxieties around an AI doomsday have been ramping up for months, and executives at top AI companies have done little to ease those worries. OpenAI’s Sam Altman said humanity could lose control of the technology. Anthropic warned that its models could be abused to create chemical weapons.

But no AI leaders have looked people dead in the eye and said they specifically are going to be killed by artificial intelligence—until now.

Enter Paul Christiano, an OpenAI board member serving on its Safety and Security Committee. Earlier this week while speaking at the AI Safety Foundation’s annual Hinton Lectures, Christiano said he believes an AI takeover is imminent and that it spells certain doom for the human race.

“For most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident,” Christiano told the crowd.

What does an AI takeover mean to Christiano? He described it as “a situation where there are AI systems pursuing goals, and those systems call the shots in the same sense that humans today call the shots and what happens on Earth.”

“If, say, you or me or Donald Trump wanted to stop them, [we] would be as ineffective as if you or me were trying to stop the U.S. military,” he added.

Christiano’s AI timeline

How soon could humanity’s AI downfall happen? Christiano predicts it could occur within the next six months, or—somewhat more reassuringly?—take up to three years.

“If we tried to develop AI along the most rapid trajectory, if we said we’re just going to build this as quickly as we can in the easiest way we can, we would be looking at something like a coin flip of an AI takeover,” he reasoned.

On the bright side, Christiano said companies are avoiding that coin flip by pacing the frontier, as Anthropic’s Dario Amodei recommended after a former employee accused both Anthropic and OpenAI of “gambling with our lives.”

However, Christiano warns that “even with realistic policy responses, the risk remains exceptionally high.”

If anything, his outlook has grown slightly more urgent since joining OpenAI’s board in September. At the time, he estimated a 4% chance of losing control of AI within a year—double the six-month minimum he floated this week—and a 15% chance within three years (odds he acknowledged are based on his subjective beliefs).

“If we build superintelligence without more robust alignment, I expect we will permanently lose control of it,” Christiano wrote in a personal statement. “If that happens then most people could die. I believe we would need domestic and international coordination to ensure global consistency and reduce risk to an acceptable level.”

#10515. A remote employee refused 160 webcam photos a day. Her employer fired her

Across the workforce, employer surveillance is growing increasingly common, even though it is widely disliked by employees. According to the American Psychological Association, employee monitoring increases workers’ stress and decreases their reported mental health. A Canadian study found that surveillance in the workplace makes employees feel more pressured, less satisfied with their job, and like their privacy is being violated.

AI may now make this problem worse. These negative outcomes are the consequences of more traditional surveillance methods like keyboard tracking and email monitoring. Considering that, what would the psychological impact be of learning that an employer will now use AI to take 160 photos of an employee’s face every day?

A recent New Jersey lawsuit alleges that an employer was trying to do just that, and fired its employee when she refused to agree to this monitoring. The plaintiff in this case, Glennis Von Sander-Timinski, worked for Sutherland Healthcare Solutions, which provides healthcare services outsourcing. The suit states that she had been working at home with no issues since 2018, and had achieved positive performance reviews during that time. 

However, everything changed in August when her company told her that they would be using a new tool: Sentinel AI. This software would take a photo of her through her webcam about every three minutes over the course of the day, for a total of about 160 photos per day.

Von Sander-Timinski objected to this with the worry that it would increase her stress level, and therefore trigger her underlying lupus. According to the Lupus Foundation of America, stress can be a significant trigger of lupus flares, which can result in fevers, rashes, and sores. Her doctor wrote a note to her employer arguing that the facial AI monitoring should be changed to be “intermittent or less frequently, as it is causing worsening of anxiety and flaring her systemic lupus erythematosus.”

However, Sutherland Healthcare was not willing to compromise and gave her an ultimatum. She could agree to the AI monitoring, come into the office every day, or be fired. Returning to the office was not feasible as she lives in Atlantic County, on the opposite side of New Jersey from her employer’s office in Clinton. The lawsuit estimated that her daily commute would have been a total of six hours long.

Therefore, on September 8, Von Sander-Timinski was fired. She had worked at Sutherland for over a decade, since it acquired the company she previously worked for in 2013. 

“Our client’s employer failed to engage in the interactive process required under the New Jersey Law Against Discrimination and denied a reasonable accommodation that would have allowed Ms. Von Sander-Timinski to continue performing her job duties successfully, as she had done for years prior to the implementation of this monitoring system,” said Von Sander-Timinski’s lawyers in a statement to The Bergen Record.

While many states currently do not have any laws against employer surveillance, some states, such as New York, Connecticut, Delaware, and California, are beginning to set boundaries for companies. Earlier this year, Maine also passed a law that bans surveillance within an employee’s home unless it is deemed necessary.

New Jersey is similarly looking to pass a law that would regulate AI electronic monitoring tools in the workplace. It would mandate that AI-powered surveillance would need to be approved by an independent auditor and would limit where and when monitoring can be active. 

While this bill is still under discussion, it could potentially help employees like Von Sander-Timinski avoid similar situations in the future. For now, in the vast majority of states, if an employer decides to implement facial monitoring, employees will have little option but to smile for the camera.

#10514. Googlebook apps built by Googlers add macOS-like status bar shortcuts, keyboard commands

Googlebooks are a bit starved of desktop-class features at launch, but one of Google’s pitches around this platform is how apps can be built for it, and the company’s own employees are showing off what that looks like with some clever apps that just so happen to add features that feel a lot like they’re replicating macOS staples.

In a Reddit thread, three Googlebook apps built by Googlers through Antigravity are shown off, and they’re pretty cool, regardless of how you might feel about the platform itself.

“BentoBox” is a utility that gives you control over the status bar on Googlebook, enabling you to fill the status bar with shortcuts, mini-apps, and more. It’s full of glancable information such as weather conditions, battery charging speeds, and more, but also includes useful tools such as being able to access a clipboard history, set a timer, and more. The app requires permissions including accessibility overlays, but it works like a charm.

I had no idea the status bar on Googlebook could even be used like this, and it really makes that space a lot more useful. Of course, you have to draw a comparison here to macOS, which also uses this space for app shortcuts and tools, though BentoBox offers a different type of customization.

BentoBox is available for download via Google Play for free.

The other Mac-like app here is “Booklight,” a launcher that’s basically Apple’s Spotlight, just for Googlebook. It has a transparent design and lets you search “apps, settings, and the web.”

Technically, Googlebook already can do this in its built-in search bar (in the app drawer), but Booklight has more customization and functionality, including being able to write out shorthand commands all in one sentence with the app then completing the command in the appropriate apps, as well as having a clearer UI for experiences such as typing in quick math equations. It’s also good at finding symbols (so you don’t have to remember the U+ codes that carried over from ChromeOS). Not one I found myself wanting to use, but the potential is there.

Both BentoBox and Booklight were developed by Alexander Kuscher, VP over Laptops & Tablets at Google.

The other app highlighted in Google’s thread was Wayfinder, a file manager app described as a “desktop-grade file manager.” The big bonus here is network file access for NAS boxes and other uses, but the app also just has a more advanced UX compared to Googlebook’s built-in Files app.

Googlebook’s app gap is a real problem at launch, but these apps do show there’s a lot of potential in the platform, it’s just a matter of getting developers on board – which itself will require Google and its partners to actually sell some of these laptops… classic chicken-and-egg situation.

#10513. Fresh European Fridge Attacks Put Cold-Chain Security in Focus

Beyond food storage, the same combination of Internet connectivity, remote access, and inadequate security practices can put temperature-controlled infrastructure across other critical sectors at risk.

A second wave of attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe this week has heightened concerns about the broader "cold chain's" vulnerability to similar attacks, given that supermarkets aren't the only businesses that rely on cold storage.

As in mid-October, an unknown threat actor appears to have gained access to refrigeration controllers at multiple European supermarkets and switched the systems to defrost mode, raising temperatures to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) and causing food spoilage.

Reporting by the BBC, Reuters, CNBC, and other outlets suggests the latest attacks were smaller in scope compared with the first wave in October that affected more than 700 retail and grocery stores, primarily in France. A smaller number of stores in Belgium, Germany, the Netherlands, Portugal, Poland and Spain were also caught up in the October attacks.

Related:How to Assess OT Incident Response Preparedness

BBC reported the new attacks as impacting "dozens of supermarkets" in seven European countries including Belgium, Luxembourg, Estonia, Ireland, Sweden and Finland. Spokespersons from several supermarket chains that include France's Carrefour, Belgium's Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt Group, and Sweden's Coop chains confirmed varying but relatively limited impacts from the new attacks.

In a Nov. 2 statement, Carrefour said a cyberattack targeting its refrigeration systems had impacted 15 out of 700 stores in Belgium. In an undated statement, US-based Copeland, which manufactures technologies for regulating commercial refrigeration systems, alluded to a cybersecurity incident affecting refrigeration systems in France, which it said related to a discontinued generation of supervisory controllers.

No individual or group has claimed responsibility for either the first or the second wave of attacks, and the motivation behind it remains a mystery. European authorities are currently investigating the attacks.

Researchers, including those at France's CERT, have linked the hacks so far to Internet-connected refrigeration controllers made by Denmark-based Danfoss, Italy-based Dixell, and Copeland. Organizations using these controllers often connect them to the Internet to enable remote maintenance and support, but in doing so also potentially expose them to unauthorized access and remote attack by threat actors.

Risks include unpatched vulnerabilities in these technologies that attackers can exploit, like three in Danfoss' AK-SM 800A controllers that researchers at Claroty disclosed this August and another two they reported the same month in Copeland controllers. Weak configurations and poor security hygiene are other major problems.

Related:Why Europe's Freezer Hacks Spread So Far, So Fast

"Misconfigurations and systemic hygiene failures represent the vast majority of the threat surface," says John Gallagher, vice president at operational technology (OT) and Internet of Things (IoT) security vendor Viakoo. "While unpatched vulnerabilities exist in older firmware, they are rendered dangerous only because basic architectural hygiene was skipped, especially [when] making them Internet-facing."

Common mistakes that include widespread use of default passwords, vendor-shared service codes, or static credentials across hundreds of locations make brute-forcing trivial, Gallagher adds.

The weaknesses are not confined to supermarket refrigeration systems. The same combination of Internet connectivity, remote access, and inadequate security practices can put temperature-controlled infrastructure across other critical sectors at risk, according to security experts.

Sean Tufts, field chief technology officer (CTO) at Claroty, points out that "pharmaceutical storage and distribution, food distribution centers, and industrial facilities all rely on connected operational technology to maintain precise environmental conditions."

Related:Les supermarchés de l'UE paient d'un firmware de réfrigérateur non mis à jour

The level of exposure will vary depending on how these systems are deployed, connected, and secured. But many organizations that rely on remotely accessible refrigeration or temperature-control equipment face similar challenges around asset visibility, third-party access, and securing legacy systems, Tufts says. "The same types of weaknesses can exist across different industries, even if the equipment and operational requirements differ."

The potential consequences of a compromise, Tufts says, can vary by sector.

"A disruption to pharmaceutical storage could compromise temperature-sensitive medicines, while an incident affecting food distribution could lead to spoilage and supply chain disruptions," he notes. "Industrial environments may face additional operational consequences depending on the materials and processes involved."

The supermarket attacks are a reminder that refrigeration and temperature-control systems are part of essential operations and not just back-of-house equipment, Tufts adds. Organizations should identify these assets and know how they connect to the Internet and third parties.

"Where remote access is necessary, use a VPN, strong authentication, or a centralized secure-access tool with session tracking." Changing default passwords, keeping firmware current, and segmenting are also recommended security practices, he says.

Gallagher says that while it's unclear how the attacks on the commercial refrigeration systems played out, the most straightforward theory is the threat actor likely compiled a target list by scanning the public Internet for specific controller fingerprints, such as those tied to Danfoss, Dixell, and Copeland. They then likely deployed an automated script across that target list to exploit known web vulnerabilities or push default credentials, triggering the defrost mode simultaneously.

Gallagher says the same attacks that worked on commercial refrigeration systems can potentially work across almost any form of OT and IoT systems. That's because these systems often are managed outside of IT, lack automated controls to keep firmware and passwords updated, and have porous network borders. "The growth over the last three years in operational ransomware and in cyberattacks causing physical damage shows that these attacks are on the rise and not specific to any one kind of system."

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.
