#10487. The most important shopper of the future isn’t human

A shopper asks an AI assistant for sneakers for a 23-year-old. Another Googles a boutique hotel in Rome. Before either sees a picture of a shoe or a room, artificial intelligence has helped decide which brands deserve consideration. Mental availability is no longer formed directly by comms and shopper experience; a new intermediary has stepped in.

AI is increasingly a gatekeeper between businesses and their customers. Shoppers don’t have to open a chatbot for AI to influence their choices. It is already embedded in familiar services. Think of Google, where AI-generated answers appear before people visit a brand’s website.

Morgan Stanley estimates that agent-influenced shopping could account for $190 billion to $385 billion in U.S. e-commerce spending by 2030, or 10% to 20% of the market. Of course, being memorable to humans is still essential, but leaders also need to consider whether their brand is understood by AI, not just people.

People can accommodate changing messages within an existing emotional attachment to a brand. Machines do not share that attachment. Fragmented messaging or unsupported claims can leave AI systems with conflicting information, making them less likely to recommend the brand. 

Even the biggest names cannot assume they will appear. Authors writing in Harvard Business Review in 2026 found that Brooks appeared more reliably than Nike in their tests of AI recommendations for running shoes.

The response requires more than trying to influence where AI looks for answers. Brands are racing to SEO, GEO, and Reddit strategies, but the landscape is continually evolving. To remain in consideration by both audiences, brands need to go back to their roots, examine their foundations, and be more disciplined in their execution. They must focus on the core idea the brand stands for and how consistently that meaning comes across wherever the brand appears.

So, how do you do it?

Design your business for humans and machines at the same time

AI does not feel your brand. It can identify the emotions associated with it, but it does not share the attachment that makes someone instinctively reach for your product.

Emotional resonance and machine legibility require a coordinated approach. The question is whether the meaning you have built around your brand is relevant to the shopper. Does it connect to the visual presence you have built, and can the machine validate it all?

Take Dove. Its real beauty message has created a powerful position around inclusion. Yet when we asked an AI assistant to recommend a good cream for sensitive skin, Dove did not appear. Asked why, the assistant associated it with affordability. The brand’s broader message had not translated into relevance to that skincare request.

KitKat has a particularly clear narrative: Take a break. It gives people a reason to reach for the brand beyond simply wanting chocolate, making KitKat come to mind when they want a pause.

Our research into AI and brand magnetism has shown that to build both mental availability and machine awareness, brands need at least three ownable distinctive assets and a clear relevant narrative. To ensure your brand is understood by AI, keep your messaging consistent across channels and over time.

Nike shows that even owning distinctive assets alone is not enough. The Swoosh and “Just Do It” make Nike instantly recognizable, yet when AI was asked to recommend a running shoe for a 23-year-old, it didn’t feature Nike in the top three. Surprising perhaps, but AI points out that competitors have built strong associations with emerging buying needs: New Balance on authenticity, Lululemon with wellness. Not only have other brands created more relevant narratives, Nike’s own is suffering from semantic contradictions: “Just do it,” “Believe in something,” “Why do it?’ Irrespective of how emotional appealing it all is to humans, the machine finds these contradictions and so will not recommend the brand.

Brands structured for this new AI-mediated world have to deal with this new complexity. Build emotional appeal for people alongside information machines can use to understand that relevance. This is the new standard of brand craft, giving creativity a sharper brief. Brands that master both early will be harder to displace.

Build through repetition, coherence, and ownable signals

Once that relevance is established, the brand itself needs to accumulate presence through repeated exposure. The same visual and verbal cues should reinforce one another across websites, retail communications, and social channels.

Research by Charlie Oscar, reported by WARC, analyzed 30 brands across six categories, and attributed 63% of LLM visibility to long-term brand equity. AI pulls from everything, so years of brand building matter. Volvo’s long-term association with safety illustrates the strength of a settled meaning, for example.

A social post may feel fresh in isolation, but if it introduces a conflicting message, it adds confusion to the brand’s wider digital footprint.

That makes marketers’ impatience expensive. Your team may be tired of a campaign long before customers have properly registered it. Internal boredom is no reason to discard an association you are still building. Familiarity takes time to build and reinforce.

Pursuing new trends becomes a trap door. The brand needs to be clear about what must not change—ownable visual assets and core narrative—and what can change: executions.

Heinz shows the value of continuity. Years ago, there was discussion about removing its keystone logo because it seemed old-fashioned. The surrounding communications could be refreshed without discarding the symbol that made the brand recognizable.

Give agencies recognizable assets to work with and a clear meaning to reinforce. Find fresh expressions of the brand. Change the shirt, change the earrings, but remain recognizably yourself.

The same discipline applies to promises. Make sure your claims reflect what your business actually does, and provide evidence to support them.

The strongest brands give people reasons to remember them and machines clear signals to work with. Build those together, consistently over time, and you give both audiences a reason to choose you.

#10486. Why New York City’s grocery store plan is not just about food

New York City is moving closer to launching its effort to counter food inflation by opening five city-run grocery stores. Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced in May 2026 that the first store would open in the Hunts Point neighborhood of the South Bronx in 2027, with another in East Harlem to follow.

Five stores, one in each borough, are unlikely to substantially change grocery prices in a city with nearly 1,000 supermarkets and more than 8 million inhabitants. But each could make a meaningful difference to the grocery bills of local shoppers by selling essentials at below-market prices.

Even with just five planned stores set to open in lower-income neighborhoods, the initiative has ignited fierce opposition from independent grocers, supermarket trade associations, and a coalition representing immigrant-owned food businesses.

What explains this pushback?

As a food policy scholar, I believe this opposition is about more than the immediate economic impact of five stores. It is about the precedent they could establish. Mamdani’s initiative challenges an entrenched expectation that the government should leave the provision of consumer goods to private enterprise even as it encourages businesses to invest in certain locations, regulates their activities, and helps low-income shoppers through various food assistance programs.

The reality is more complicated. For at least a century, New York’s food economy has not operated independently of government. In fact, public policies and investments have long shaped where supermarkets open, which businesses can operate with a profit, and how residents obtain food.

It’s just that they have done so in ways consumers often don’t see.

That is why the five grocery stores carry a broader significance, in my view. They offer a different model of public investment that makes the government much more visible in providing an essential service—and more accountable for its results. New Yorkers will get an opportunity to judge that contribution directly.

If the stores succeed, they may change not just what people expect to pay for groceries, but what they expect their city government to provide.

How the plan will work

New York City has committed $70 million to develop these stores, which will be open to all.

While they will be managed by private operators, the city will provide rent-free space, prioritize publicly owned sites, and ensure that essential foods are priced 30% below typical retail prices.

In this respect, the stores offer a “public option”—a government-provided good or service that exists alongside private alternatives, like public schools and city hospitals.

Municipal grocery stores would offer New Yorkers a similar choice alongside private retailers. But as a public option, they would create a visible alternative against which shoppers can judge privately owned stores, setting a benchmark for food prices and service quality. They would also demonstrate how public investment can be used to make an essential good more affordable.

At his May announcement, Mamdani described the proposed Bronx store and its surrounding development as “physical proof of our conviction that government can be a force for good.”

A fresh form of intervention

Government-supported food retailing has a long history in New York City despite opposition by existing businesses.

In 1934, Mayor Fiorello La Guardia’s administration began selling discounted milk to low-income families, but the initiative drew complaints from grocers about unfair competition. Independent merchants similarly protested the city’s efforts to subsidize a new Pathmark supermarket in East Harlem in the 1990s, warning that it would put local grocers out of business.

A more recent example is the city’s Food Retail Expansion to Support Health program, known as FRESH. Since 2009, it has offered supermarket developers and operators long-term tax breaks and zoning incentives to build or expand dozens of stores in underserved neighborhoods.

These incentives have helped increase grocery retail space, but shoppers don’t see the public support behind them.

FRESH is just one example of an approach toward supermarket financing that gained momentum in the 1990s, when governments sought to address social problems by encouraging private investment. Food insecurity was blamed on a scarcity of neighborhood supermarkets, not on prices being beyond reach for local shoppers.

Subsidizing new stores promised better nutrition and economic development without confronting poverty or inequality, and FRESH reflects that approach. Participating supermarkets must devote space to perishable foods, but they’re not required to offer affordable prices. That may be one reason why researchers have found that adding supermarkets to low-income neighborhoods, by itself, doesn’t substantially improve residents’ diets.

This hidden government role is hardly confined to grocery stores. Much of what government does for Americans is delivered indirectly, through tax credits, subsidies, and private institutions. Because the public contribution is obscured, people often give credit to private markets for the benefits provided by public policy, from student loans to healthcare.

This invisibility is a consequence of policy design and influences how citizens understand government, a phenomenon that political scientist Suzanne Mettler described as “the submerged state.”

Bringing the state into the open

Municipal grocery stores depart from the traditional model in two important ways.

First, they make affordability an explicit condition of public investment rather than the outcome of increased retail competition. Second, they make government’s contribution visible. For example, the stores will share distinct branding so shoppers know who’s responsible for the affordable food.

If the stores deliver reliable savings, shoppers may begin to see affordable food as something government can help provide, not an outcome determined entirely by private markets. When public benefits are obscured, people are more likely to underestimate government’s contribution to their lives. Visible programs, like a physical store in the neighborhood, make that contribution easier to notice and evaluate.

Visibility also creates accountability. A customer at a private supermarket that received a tax break to expand isn’t likely to tie the store’s prices or food quality to government policy. At a municipal grocery store, with clear branding, the connection is unmistakable.

To be sure, critics’ concerns deserve serious attention. Many independent grocery stores are owned by immigrant entrepreneurs operating on thin margins. Groups representing bodegas and independent supermarkets warn that a publicly subsidized competitor could draw away their customers. Some may lose business.

Yet East Harlem’s Pathmark demonstrates that new supermarkets and smaller retailers can coexist. Between 2000 and 2015, the number of small grocery stores and bodegas in the neighborhood increased from 100 to 126, while supermarkets rose from 10 to 18. That said, those figures don’t establish Pathmark’s effects on individual businesses.

The municipal stores’ impact on nearby retailers remains an open question. But the task for New York City is to ensure that private operators deliver excellent service and real savings, and that their commercial interests don’t undermine the public mission. It will also need to provide good working conditions and track effects on nearby businesses.

Ultimately, public ownership doesn’t guarantee success. But it makes the government’s responsibility for the outcome impossible to miss.

Nevin Cohen is a chair of the Department of Health Policy and Management at the CUNY Graduate School of Public Health and Public Policy.

#10484. Samsung’s paid Galaxy AI plan has a giant Gemini problem

Good morning. Today I’m trying desperately not to buy Sony’s new nostalgia-bait headphones, reeling from how emotionally invested I was in Spider-Man: Brand New Day (yes, I know I’m late), trying to figure out what a “private, agentic notebook” is, and slowly coming around to the idea of the New York Times owning Letterboxd.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

The relationship between Samsung and Google has, over the years, waxed and waned depending on their respective interdependence. Samsung is Android’s physical emissary, powering a plurality of all its handsets globally. But Google, and in particular its services, is the glue that holds Samsung’s smartphone experience together.

The back and forth is over a decade old; back in early 2014, Samsung shipped a refreshed magazine-style skin with its Galaxy tablets that eschewed many of the design tenets Google had been pushing its partners to adhere to. Not only was Samsung willfully defying its most important partner, but it made a point of barely mentioning Android during its press conferences.

Around the same time, it transitioned its smartwatches from Android Wear to Tizen and began shipping duplicative apps on its devices (many of which persist to this day). The goal was to distance itself from Google as much as possible.

While we don’t know exactly what happened behind closed doors, we saw the outcome quite clearly: Magazine UX lasted one product cycle, and the two companies signed a 10-year cross-license patent deal, which may have helped Samsung prevent any future lawsuits with Apple. Google then sold Motorola to Lenovo, clearing the way for Samsung to continue building its burgeoning hardware business on the back of Google’s mobile ecosystem.

Since then, the two companies have grown even closer. In 2021, they co-announced a new Wear OS along with an overarching wearables partnership that has since grown to include Android XR as well. And Google is still the default search engine for Samsung devices, despite reported inroads made by Microsoft in 2023 to convince the Korean giant to switch to a ChatGPT-powered version of Bing Search. (Samsung’s ongoing relationship with Microsoft, which bundles its Office suite on most Galaxy devices, could be seen as a point of leverage for negotiations with Google, too.)

This brings us to today, and to AI. Samsung was among the first companies to adopt Google’s full suite of Gemini Intelligence products, and its phones often get new AI features before anyone else. But like a decade ago, when Samsung shipped Bixby to kind-of-sort-of compete with Google Assistant, it still wants to offer its own services alongside Google’s.

So a rumor that Samsung may launch a paid Galaxy AI Premium subscription next year for $5/month piqued my interest for the same reason Magazine UX did 12 years ago. Galaxy AI features today are a blend of first-party and third-party capabilities, but none of them are especially useful, particularly when compared to Google’s own Android equivalents powered by Gemini Intelligence. Now Bar and Now Brief, two heavily promoted features in Samsung’s marketing, are wildly disappointing.

At I/O this past May, Google announced Spark, an agent that goes out and performs actions on your behalf. And while it’s since been somewhat eclipsed by more capable mobile options like Meta’s Muse, it’s obvious that Google is working on a follow-up that will perform functions both on the phone and inside apps.

That’s exactly what Samsung is rumored to be working on with Bixby Action, a spiritual successor to its namesake that, when it debuted, prioritized on-device tasks like turning on Wi-Fi over web-based actions Google Assistant did better.

According to leaks from SamMobile, Galaxy AI Premium will offer agentic upgrades for phone users to “create commands triggers and system routines for daily tasks” or “automate routine daily tasks using Galaxy AI.” Gen Video will reportedly “convert static photos into dynamic video clips,” while a new Daily Briefing likely does what it says on the tin.

Will Samsung users see enough value in this hodgepodge of features paywalled only because they use a surfeit of compute? And what models will power them on the backend?

Right now, Google is in the enviable position of being able to offer its AI at three distinct layers: the model itself, which is invisible to the user; the OS level, which can promulgate Gemini across every Android phone that runs Google services; and the hardware level, where Pixel lets it specialize and optimize.

Samsung, not particularly known for its software prowess, will likely need to step gingerly around Google’s AI shadow while also justifying the cost to shore up its much-needed services revenue. Based on this leaked roadmap, though, I’m not confident it will work out.

Instead, Samsung may want to acquire one of the many up-and-coming AI agent startups whose valuations are rising more quickly than their user bases. While Muse and OpenAI’s Dots have taken up most of the recent conversation, I’ve been using Hark, Town, and Instinct pretty regularly for a month or so and could see them being brought in-house by Samsung and offered either as standalone products or customized for Galaxy devices. As Google is doing with its own AI plans, Samsung could provide Galaxy users a year of free service, after which they would be expected to pay.

Samsung doesn’t have a great history of building software, but many of its acquisitions, from SmartThings to Viv Labs (which became “next-gen” Bixby) to LoopPay (which became Samsung Pay) to Whisk (which became Samsung Food), have proven successful. Given the current urgent state of mobile AI, I’d forgo the hodgepodge and bring in some outside expertise.

Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy is the only thing tech media can talk about right now, likely because it has implications far beyond just Nvidia’s stock price. The Nvidia CEO, who is one of the world’s richest and most powerful tech executives, is believed to have been targeted by Chinese intelligence to potentially influence American trade policy around AI.

Alex Kantrowitz’s Big Technology piece is a useful starting point for why this matters at a global scale:

Beyond the affair, the real issue is that Huang’s love interest, ex-Megaspeed International executive Alice Huang, is someone the United States government believes passed information to the Chinese government while building data centers with Nvidia’s help in Asia. There’s simply no getting away from this detail. This isn’t just an affair, it’s a corporate and national security issue.

Whether Huang can survive the impending investigation by Nvidia’s board remains to be seen, but the CEO has been a stalwart in the tech space for 33 years, and there is no clear successor to his position should he be forced to resign.

Damien reviewed DroidDeck, which I wrote about last week as part of a broader look at Android’s gaming renaissance.

Over the last few days, things have become even more preposterous: the Ocarina of Time remake, which was released on Thursday, has already been recompiled to run natively on Android (though it runs better on PC), largely with the help of frontier AI models.

All of these AI-powered shenanigans come after Anthropic said it would stop making it possible to recreate copies of games, claiming that “recreating someone else’s specific game using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy.” Good thing there are no other models capable of doing the same thing.

I think when you zoom out and look at production, AI really has the potential to be the biggest creative unlock in modern history. The last time we saw anything close to this was really the, you know, advent of CGI and digital composites in the early ’90s. That technology gave birth to amazing stories like Jurassic Park and Terminator 2, and it’s hard to imagine that AI is not going to have a more significant impact than that. And I personally believe that’s going to be an incredible unlock on creativity.

—David Ellison, Skydance CEO, when asked about how AI could impact the movie-making process

Thanks for reading, and have a great day. I’ll talk to you on Thursday.

#10483. The chip war never ended

It’s no secret that the world runs on computer chips. 

This became clear during the pandemic, when a race for even basic chips needed to operate cars and other devices set back manufacturing timelines across the world. Beltway policymakers are reminded of just how important semiconductors are to the world every time China seems to move toward invading Taiwan, which raises the specter that the country could subsume control of TSCM, the most prominent computer chip contract manufacturer. 

Now Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia, which comes after reports of at least three known extramarital affairs—one of them with an alleged spy for the Chinese government—has thrown the world’s supply of computer chips back in the spotlight. With stocks falling and no obvious succession plan, it’s not clear what the future of Nvidia is right now, or how it might jostle the broader semiconductor ecosystem. 

“Many companies that have in the past relied on Nvidia will be watching very carefully to see whether they can rely on Nvidia going forward, and if not, they might turn to competitors,” says Chris Miller, a Tufts University professor and author of the 2022 book Chip War, which documents how the world came to depend on these tiny components.

Fast Company chatted with Miller on November 12 about Washington, D.C.’s response to the Huang scandal, Nvidia’s future, and the prospect of keeping advanced semiconductors out of countries like China. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

You’ve followed the chip industry for quite a long time. Are you surprised by what’s happened over the last few weeks? 

Jensen was an extraordinary CEO for 33 years, since Nvidia’s founding. [He] deserves a lot of the credit for the company’s extraordinary rise, but also deserves a lot of the blame for a series of poor decisions that have led not just to his ouster, but to a period of crisis for the company. Jensen really was central to Nvidia’s success, and he ran the company in a pretty unique way. He had 60 different people reporting to him directly, so there wasn’t a sort of standard corporate hierarchy, which worked really well for a long time. 

But it means that now that he’s gone, it’s not obvious who can fill his shoes. There’s not really a deputy who was waiting in the wings to take over. 

I’m curious about the history of espionage attempts like what’s being alleged here. 

There is some history during the Cold War, for example. There were efforts by spies from the Soviet Union or Eastern European countries to get access to sensitive technology by getting close to semiconductor executives. But I think the scale of this is kind of unique. First, that it happened to such a central company in the U.S. tech ecosystem, the most valuable company in the world. That’s somewhat unique. 

The second thing that’s unique is that the affair in question was both with a major customer, which shouldn’t have happened, as well as an [alleged] Chinese intelligence asset. There were a series of failures of judgment for a person who was one of the most important people in the U.S. and really in the entire world’s technology sector, and that combination does make this case unique.

I’m wondering about unexpected winners or companies that stand to benefit from this happening, especially other companies in the GPU market.

There are going to be competitors of Nvidia that will see this as an opportunity to win market share. AMD, for example, produces GPUs like Nvidia. In addition, many of Nvidia’s key customers, firms like Amazon—which has a vast data center business—buy Nvidia GPUs, but also design their own chips that have comparable performance characteristics. 

Many companies that have in the past relied on Nvidia will be watching very carefully to see whether they can rely on Nvidia going forward, and if not, they might turn to competitors.

Some leaders on the left are arguing this scandal is made worse because there’s so much market concentration in the semiconductor sector, that we’re too dependent on a small set of companies. Does that ring true to you?  

The market’s concentrated right now, but it’s a market that is also highly competitive. It’s worth remembering the market for AI chips scarcely existed five years ago when ChatGPT was launched. . . . I think what we’re going to see over the next couple of months is that if Nvidia does face a prolonged period of distraction and chaos, competitors to Nvidia are going to win market share.

I would look at this as actually a quite competitive market with a bunch of different players that all have pretty advanced capabilities.

Is it feasible to wall off technology from China? I know Nvidia was even considering putting location tracking in some of its chips to keep them away from certain places, even if they’re sold on the gray or black market.

One of the ironies of this is that Nvidia, in general, and Jensen in particular, thought they could play a big role in dictating Washington’s technology policy and were naive to the fact that China was playing them by [allegedly] turning Jensen’s mistress into an intelligence agent. 

This is going to lead to a major reduction in Nvidia’s influence in Washington. Its influence in the White House is declining as well, and I think Washington will respond with tighter controls over where chips can be sent and which types of companies are allowed to buy large numbers of these chips when it comes to installing them in foreign countries.

#10481. AI is making software easier to build. Keeping it running is another story

These days, it almost feels like old news: Developers can now use AI tools to generate code, build features, and make changes in a fraction of the time they once needed. The problem now surfacing across businesses is that once software goes into production, teams still need to monitor, maintain, and fix it. A feature that takes minutes to build can introduce problems that take engineers hours to investigate.

Google’s 2025 DORA report, based on responses from nearly 5,000 technology professionals, found that greater AI adoption was associated with faster software delivery but reduced stability. While the researchers didn’t establish that AI-generated code directly caused more outages, their findings suggest that companies can produce software faster without necessarily becoming better at maintaining it.

That raises a critical question for companies investing heavily in AI coding tools: If development keeps getting faster, how much of the work involved in running software can also be automated? A growing group of companies is working to find out, developing AI systems that can investigate failures, identify possible causes, and, in some cases, take corrective action without waiting for an engineer.

MORE SOFTWARE, MORE TO MANAGE

Ishay Yaari, cofounder and CEO of DataAgent, a company developing autonomous remediation software, says the operational side of software development hasn’t advanced at the same pace as coding.

“More code, more frequent deployments, and more infrastructure changes naturally create more potential failure points,” he tells Fast Company.

For site reliability engineering (SRE) teams, that means managing applications and infrastructure that may be changing more frequently. When something fails, engineers must figure out what changed, identify the cause, and restore service.

Consider an application that begins crashing after an update. The cause could be faulty code, an incorrect configuration, insufficient computing resources, or a problem with another service. While monitoring tools may detect the failure immediately, engineers still need to examine logs, review recent changes, and investigate several possibilities before deciding what to fix.

Yaari says companies often respond to growing complexity by adding monitoring tools and collecting more data. That can help engineers see what’s happening, but it can also mean more alerts to investigate without necessarily improving how quickly problems are resolved.

The pressure isn’t necessarily coming from poor-quality AI-generated code. Even reliable code can be difficult to manage when applications, infrastructure, and dependencies are changing frequently.

In a recent analysis of AI-assisted development, Google’s DORA researchers found that developers saved time generating code but spent more time reviewing and verifying it. They also emphasized the importance of testing, feedback, and established engineering practices in turning faster development into better results.

For companies, that means the benefits of AI coding tools may depend partly on what happens after developers finish writing the code, particularly the ability of SRE teams to keep applications running reliably.

GIVING AI THE KEYS TO PRODUCTION

Software monitoring and observability tools have traditionally helped engineers detect problems and understand their causes. Now companies are trying to automate more of the response.

DataAgent is pursuing that approach. Its platform is designed to monitor applications and cloud infrastructure, identify potential issues, and help investigate them. Yaari wants AI to take on more of the operational work engineers currently perform manually.

Some failures have familiar remedies. An application might repeatedly crash because it doesn’t have enough memory. A deployment might fail because of an incorrect configuration. Or a new release might introduce errors that disappear when the system returns to an earlier version.

Companies already use automation to address certain problems through predefined rules. AI could extend that capability by examining the circumstances, identifying likely causes, and selecting an appropriate response.

Yaari says DataAgent’s platform is designed to understand both the infrastructure supporting an application and the application itself, including how services interact, what the application is expected to do, and how its behavior changes after an update.

The aim is to recognize problems that don’t fit a predefined rule. But identifying a likely solution is one thing. Allowing software to make changes to a live application is another.

Consider a deployment that introduces errors. Rolling back to the previous version may restore service, but if the update also changed a database or introduced new dependencies, reversing it could create additional problems. That’s why the ability to act matters as much as the ability to diagnose.

HOW MUCH SHOULD AI BE ALLOWED TO FIX?

In its 2026 State of AI-First Operations report, PagerDuty found that 44% of surveyed organizations required human involvement when AI was used to fix problems affecting customer-facing systems, while 43% required it when coordinating incident responses across teams.

Even companies adopting AI for operational work appear reluctant to give it unrestricted authority over critical systems.

Yaari agrees that some decisions should remain with people. He points to actions such as deleting large amounts of data, disabling security controls, or exposing sensitive information as examples that should require approval.

“The goal is not to remove humans from SRE; it is to remove humans from the repetitive operational work that machines can handle safely,” he says.

Companies must determine which systems an AI agent can access, what changes it can make, and when it must request approval. They also need records of what the agent did, particularly when an attempted fix fails.

Another consideration is the cost of monitoring and observability software. Applications generate vast amounts of logs, performance measurements, and other operational data. Companies pay to collect, store, and analyze that information, often across several platforms. Adding AI can create further expenses if it requires transferring large amounts of data to external services.

Yaari argues that more analysis should happen closer to where applications run. DataAgent is pursuing a distributed approach, with agents deployed within customers’ infrastructure to reduce the amount of data sent elsewhere.

Its published documentation describes local monitoring alongside cloud-based AI analysis and guided incident investigation. Yaari’s responses describe broader autonomous remediation capabilities. The company has not provided independent performance data establishing how much operational work or cost those capabilities can eliminate.

WHAT HAPPENS TO THE ENGINEER?

Yaari expects engineers to spend less time investigating repetitive incidents and more time designing systems, setting operational policies, and deciding what automated tools should be allowed to do.

“The fundamental shift is from people operating infrastructure to people managing autonomous infrastructure,” he says.

That could allow smaller engineering teams to support more applications, but it would also require them to understand how automated systems make decisions—and what happens when those decisions are wrong.

Engineering skills may evolve as a result. System architecture, security, reliability, and the ability to investigate unusual failures could become more important as routine operational work becomes easier to automate.

Google’s DORA research found that organizations with strong engineering practices were better positioned to benefit from AI-assisted development. The same lesson may apply to AI-powered operations. Companies will still need reliable processes for testing changes, responding to incidents, and evaluating whether automated fixes work.

The software industry has made considerable progress in helping developers produce code faster. Now it’s trying to bring some of that speed to keeping applications running.

If AI eventually handles both, engineers may spend less time performing individual tasks and more time deciding what the systems they build should do, how they should behave, and when a person needs to intervene.

#10479. Meta issues a high-priority update to prevent some glasses from getting ‘too warm’ when wet [U]

The latest Meta Glasses (not Ray-Ban or Oakley-branded) may temporarily overheat if they get too wet, but a software patch is here to help prevent that.

Folks using Meta Glasses in the Adventurer, Fury, Starfire, Nova, or Capri styles should open the Meta AI app on their smartphones and get their glasses updated as soon as possible. Meta sent out an email to all Glasses owners noting that the company has “an important software update” related to performance when “excessive moisture or sweat” enters the device. Meta specifically says this issue does not affect Ray-Ban or Oakley-branded Meta glasses.

Meta sent out an email to all Meta Glasses owners with the tagline “Action required,” noting that this could be a potentially serious issue:

“We’ve implemented a software update to fix a rare issue that caused a small number of Meta Glasses to get too warm when moisture entered the device. It works similarly to a phone shutting off automatically when it needs to cool down. If people experience this, they can contact Meta Customer Service for a replacement.”

The new software update brings your glasses to version 130, which includes a special software hook that shuts them down if they were to get too warm. Meta told me that the temperature for this threshold is quite low, and that the glasses shut off to prevent any potential issues. The company was very specific about the wording in the statement, carefully using the word “warm” instead of “hot,” so as to avoid the stigma that comes with that term on wearable technology.

While I haven’t seen any specific reports of Meta’s newest glasses models overheating, there are plenty of Reddit threads citing overheating issues on Ray-Ban Meta glasses over the years. #10477. Thinking of quitting your job? Don’t until you consider this factor

You know that stinging sensation you get when your coworker gets the promotion that you thought was yours? Or that sinking feeling of doom when you realize that a new hire could take over your role? Most likely, that voice within will tell you: “You’re falling behind.”

You are, however, likely ignoring an important emotional experience happening at the same time. It’s envy: simply wanting something that someone else has. Because of the stigma and shame attached to this “deadly sin,” we tend to want to suppress envy without even knowing it. It’s understandable, but also a huge inadvertent mistake.

If you’re a conscientious high achiever, or someone smart and caring, it is easy to see someone else’s success and start questioning your situation. Envy is a universal emotion. It is also normal to wonder if it’s time to make a big change, like looking for a new job or even a new career. But examining your envy first can help you avoid costly career pitfalls.

Beware of ‘Premature Game Switching’

A common reaction to workplace envy that I see among my coaching clients is to make a change. This feels like being proactive, but it is giving up on the current situation too soon, or what I call “premature game switching.” You see someone getting ahead or getting what you want in the game you’re playing. You jump the gun and assess that you can’t obtain what you want or win at this game, so you opt out and choose a different contest.

Doing something feels better than doing nothing. When we avoid taking a beat to study our envy, however, we ignore critical data.

All negative emotions have what is called “signaling value,” demanding that we pay attention to what is important. Fear helps us see danger. Grief occurs when we lose someone dear. Envy helps us see what we truly desire and avoid “desire confusion.”

Thanks to savvy advertisers and social media, we are inundated with opportunities to feel what the philosopher and critic René Girard called “mimetic desire.” We tend to want things that those around us want. While “keeping up with the Joneses” used to include only neighbors or people we encounter in real life, the blast radius for envy has widened. Now we can see many more things that many more people have. We don’t often see how these cloud our judgment.

Envy gives us a chance to see what we really want.

Heed the SIReN

To examine envy, start by looking at its four key components, or “SIReN.”

First, S is “similar target.” According to the social psychologist Abraham Tesser’s Self-Evaluation Maintenance model, we tend to compare ourselves to those who are just ahead of us, our peers or our coworkers. We envy them, while we admire those far beyond us. This provides hope, telling us that we’re not as behind as we think we are. You feel envious of the promotion, for example, because it was within your reach.

Second, I is “intangible desire.” What we truly want is not the thing itself but the feelings we believe we will experience once we have it. It isn’t really the promotion, but what it represents to you, which could be a variety of things: financial security, recognition as an expert, or the opportunity to mentor others.

Third, Re stands for “relevant comparison.” We envy in domains or areas that are important to us. If we care about our careers, we’re likely to experience career envy. It pinpoints more specifically what matters to us and where we may want to focus more energy. I, for example, don’t envy people who have podcasts, but I do envy other nonfiction authors.

Finally, N is “negative emotion.” The unpleasant feeling is a gauge. If we’re able to close the app and forget about what we saw, the envy was fleeting and perhaps not worth dwelling on. If it lingers long after you put down your smartphone, you may want to take another look at why you’re feeling that way.

Next, Channel Envy in the Right Direction

Social scientists, including Jens Lange and Jan Crusius, have shown there are two kinds of envy: benign and malicious. Malicious envy tends to occur when you’re preoccupied with the person who has what you want, while benign envy is when you focus on what it is that you want. The Right Reverend Allen Shin, Bishop Suffragan of the Episcopal Diocese of New York, recently said that with malicious envy you cede your agency to the person you envy. But when you try to figure out how to get what you want, you keep your agency.

After examining your envy and figuring out the intangible desire, the next step is to figure out some “skill-building microactions.” Ask yourself: “What tiny activities should I test out to see if I can get closer to what I want?” If, for example, you realize that the intangible desire from wanting a promotion is financial security, then quitting your job will likely become a costly error. Instead, boosting your personal finance acumen might be a better option. Or, if you’re realizing that a promotion to you means mentoring others, then perhaps learning how to get reengaged with your alumni association and finding ways to mentor younger alumni might be a way to get more immediate satisfaction.

Finally, when we can direct our envy toward meaningful work, deepening relationships and serving others, we can feel more satisfied with our lives and do some good.

Once media has been backed up to Google Photos, Samsung Gallery also now has a “free up space” button that can delete the local copies of your photos and videos to open up storage on your phone.

#10471. Prompt Management in TypeScript: LangSmith vs Git vs 3 Open-Source Registries

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Every prompt registry we tested can change a prompt in a running TypeScript app, roll it back, and give production and staging different versions. LangSmith's prompt hub, Langfuse, Phoenix and AcruxCore all passed those three tests. The real differences show up elsewhere: which template syntax each one accepts, how many npm packages it pulls in, how long a change takes to reach the app, and what happens when the registry is down.

We tested all of this with one small app and one prompt, which has a condition and a loop. Git files served as the baseline. Every number below comes from a recorded run.

Most teams start with prompts in code: a template string, or a .txt file next to the code that uses it. That works until a product manager wants to change one sentence, and the change has to wait for a full release.

A prompt registry moves the text out of the deploy. The app fetches the prompt by name and by a label such as production. You change which version the label points to, and the app picks up the new text without a deploy.

LangSmith's prompt hub is the best-known registry, but it is not the only one. Several of the LangSmith alternatives also manage prompts, and three of them are open source and self-hostable: Langfuse, Phoenix and AcruxCore. We covered how those tools handle tracing in Self-Hosted LangSmith Alternatives: 4 Tools Tested on One TypeScript Agent. This article covers prompts only.

Every tool got the same prompt, support-reply. Its template takes three variables: a customer name, a plan, and a list of help articles. It has one condition: a priority line appears only for premium customers. It also has one loop: one line per help article. In Jinja2 syntax, the template looks like this:

One help article contains the text Settings > Export. We included it on purpose, to catch any tool that HTML-escapes > into >.

Every tool then ran the same sequence from a TypeScript script:

Each tool used its own documented TypeScript SDK. The four registries passed all six steps. The rest of this article covers how each one got there, and what it cost.

Keeping prompts in the repository costs almost nothing. The template sits in prompts/support-reply.njk, and nunjucks, the JavaScript port of Jinja2, renders it:

The autoescape: false line matters. Our first version called nunjucks.renderString() directly, and the test failed. The default environment HTML-escapes its output, so Settings > Export reached the model as Settings > Export. Escaping is correct for web pages and wrong for prompts.

Git gives you full Jinja2, code review on every prompt change, and history in the same place as the code. What it can't do is change a prompt in a running app. Every edit, and every rollback, waits for a deploy.

LangSmith stores a prompt as a serialized LangChain object (ChatPromptTemplate), not as plain text. LangSmith's own documentation says you must use the LangChain npm package to pull prompts in TypeScript (Manage prompts programmatically). So a plain TypeScript app that uses the openai package still needs langchain and @langchain/core:

Those three packages installed 23 packages and 70 MB. Most of the size is @langchain/* (27 MB) and js-tiktoken (22 MB).

Templates. In TypeScript, LangChain accepts f-string and mustache templates. Mustache sections ({{#docs}}…{{/docs}}) handled our loop. Mustache has no ==, though, so the premium check became an is_premium boolean computed in code. We also tried templateFormat: "jinja2", which LangChain's Python package supports. In TypeScript it threw DEFAULT_PARSER_MAPPING[templateFormat] is not a function.

Labels and rollback. production and staging are reserved tags, and the documentation moves them in the UI. The langsmith JavaScript client has no public method that moves a tag. Our script called the same REST route the SDK uses internally (POST /api/v1/repos/-//tags). It worked, but it is not a documented API.

Caching. The SDK caches prompts for 300 seconds by default. In our test, a running app saw the new version 300 seconds after we moved the tag.

Langfuse's TypeScript client is one package, @langfuse/client. It installed 5 packages and 8 MB:

Creating a version, moving a label and reading by label are all public SDK calls: prompt.create, prompt.update and prompt.get (Get started with prompt management).

Templates. The documentation shows only {{variable}} substitution. But compile() calls the mustache library, so sections worked for our loop. The type signature accepts only string values, so passing a list needed a cast. The Langfuse UI colours the section tags red, and it lists title and body as the prompt's variables, not docs or is_premium. We would not depend on behaviour the documentation doesn't promise. When we sent the Jinja2 version instead, Langfuse returned the {% if %} and {% for %} tags unchanged, with no error. The model would have received them as text.

Caching. The cache time is 60 seconds by default (Caching). Our app saw the change after 62 seconds. Langfuse is also the only client with a fallback option: a prompt string the SDK uses when it cannot reach the server on a cold start.

Phoenix's TypeScript client fetches a prompt by name and tag, and toSDK() converts it into the message format the openai package expects. Phoenix templates only replace variables, so the condition and the loop have to run in your code before rendering:

That is 16 lines, against 6 to 8 for the other registries. All the extra lines are template logic that now lives in the app.

Templates. Phoenix offers MUSTACHE, F_STRING and NONE formats (Prompts reference). Even in MUSTACHE mode, though, rendering is a plain replacement of {{name}}. When we sent mustache sections, they came back unchanged, with no error.

Errors. getPrompt() catches every error, logs it and returns null. You can see this in the client source, src/utils/getPromptBySelector.ts. A missing prompt and an unreachable server look the same to your code, which is why the snippet checks for null.

Size and caching. The client installed 57 packages and 90 MB. Most of that is OpenTelemetry, which comes in through its @arizeai/phoenix-otel dependency. The client has no prompt cache, so every render is a network call. That is also why a label change showed up immediately: 0 seconds in our test.

AcruxCore stores Jinja2 templates and renders them on the server with nunjucks. The SDK sends the variables and gets back finished messages:

The template from the test section works as it is, condition and loop included, with no is_premium flag computed in code. A label is called an alias here, and promoteAlias() moves it (Manage prompts via the SDK). The SDK installed 3 packages and 12 MB. Most of the 12 MB is one OpenTelemetry package, @opentelemetry/semantic-conventions.

Templates. Jinja2 only. When we committed the mustache version, AcruxCore rejected it at commit time with Template parse error: unexpected token: #. That is a clear error, but it also means that moving mustache prompts from LangSmith or Langfuse requires rewriting them.

We sent the same two templates, a Jinja2 one and a mustache one, to each tool's own renderer:

The rows that matter most are the ones where the tags were left in the output, because those failures produce no error. The model receives raw template syntax, and the only symptom is a strange answer. Whatever tool you pick, test one prompt with logic in it before you move the rest.

Putting logic in the template is not automatically better. It lets someone change the condition without a deploy. It also lets them break the condition without a deploy. Keeping logic in code, as Phoenix forces you to do, puts every branch under code review and in your tests.

A registry is a new runtime dependency, so we tested an outage. The app reached each registry through a local proxy, and we switched the proxy off. A separate process then started while the registry was still unreachable.

LangSmith, Langfuse and AcruxCore keep serving the last good version while the registry is down, even after the cache time has passed. The risk is a cold start: a new container or a serverless function that boots during the outage. Langfuse's fallback option is the built-in answer to that. With the other tools, keep a copy of each prompt in your code as a fallback, which brings back part of the Git setup.

Keep prompts in Git if engineers make every prompt change and your deploys are quick. Set autoescape: false, and you get Jinja2, reviews and history for free.

Use LangSmith's prompt hub if you already use LangChain, or already trace with LangSmith. If your app doesn't use LangChain, budget for the extra dependency and for the tag moves that only the UI supports.

Use Langfuse if you want a small client, a local compile(), and a fallback for cold starts. Keep to {{variable}} substitution unless you are comfortable relying on mustache behaviour that the documentation doesn't promise.

Use Phoenix if you already use it for tracing, or if you prefer all template logic in code. Remember the null check, and that every render is a network call.

Use AcruxCore if you want real conditions and loops in the template and rendering on the server. Expect one network call per new set of variables, and a personal API key for writes.

Before you choose, run one of your own prompts with real logic in it through the tool's SDK, not through its playground. Two of the four registries we tested failed on template syntax without any error, and an SDK run is where you would see that.

#10466. Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

An unknown operator appears to have exfiltrated SQL Server backups from the Philippine Overseas Employment Administration in under a half hour.

An unknown threat actor managed to gain access to sensitive databases belonging to the Philippine Overseas Employment Administration, exfiltrating nearly 69GB of information on workers, contracts, and financial records, according to an analysis of a staging server used in the breach.

Over 24 minutes, the attacker copied 27 backup databases with information on overseas-employment case management, including accreditation, contracts, and cashier and LandBank records, according to threat intelligence firm Hunt.io's Oct. 28 analysis of the logs found on a Singaporean staging server used by the attacker. The cyberattackers used privileged escalation tools, namely GodPotato and SeImpersonate, and the Impacket network library for Python to move the data, but the trail stopped at the staging server, says Esteban Borges, head of research for Hunt.io.

The server had been accessed later, but by whom is not clear, Borges says. While Hunt.io has not yet discovered the data as advertised for sale, the information may have been detected and removed, but that seems unlikely, he says.

Related:State Bank of India Suffers a Customer PII Data Leak

"I won't claim the backups stopped on the staging server," he says, so it's "still a breach, since the data was copied out of the agency’s control and the log shows the transfer completing."

This is not the first time that cybersecurity firms have found evidence that Philippine government data had been stolen. In August, Hunt.io discovered another threat actor's workspace hosting a number of tools and, in that case, 1.2GB of data stolen from a Philippine nuclear regulatory agency and a maritime shipbuilding contractor. A year ago, Philippine police arrested the mayor of a small town after discovering she was a Chinese national posing as a Filipina citizen and operating a cyber-scam center.

Whether the current incident involved China or cybercriminal groups is not clear. While Hunt.io did find some Chinese language fragments in the parts of the code, that code belonged to a third-party software library; thus, Hunt.io did not attribute the hack. The company did say, however, that both cybercriminals and nation-state adversaries would find value in the personally identifiable information (PII).

"That kind of migrant-worker PII, plus contract and payment data, is useful for fraud and identity theft, so it has commercial value," Borges says. "It's also a detailed map of a diaspora population, which can interest a state actor."

The latest insight into attacks on the Philippine government came after Hunt.io researchers discovered an open directory on a server hosted on the Singaporean address space of a Helsinki-based firm, UpCloud Ltd., the analysis stated. The open directory contained tools and log files for the attack, including a rebranded version of the GodPotato privilege escalation library, a PowerShell stager to unpack tools in memory, and the full Impacket Python environment.

Related:Russian Influence Operation Widely Targets Latin America

While Hunt.io considered the incident a confirmed compromise, the lack of runtime telemetry meant that Borges could not answer where the attacker moved the data.

"[W]e still can’t answer ... how they got in, whether the payload ran, and where the data went," he says.

However, the tools and the attacker's process indicated an operator with some strong ability, but who also made some simple mistakes, Borges says.

"The payload engineering is competent, [but] the operational security is poor — they left the staging server and its logs wide open," he says. "[It was] someone who can build the tool properly but was careless about keeping their own server quiet. I wouldn't call that top-tier or amateur."

The impact of the breach may boil down to the identity of the attacker and what they do with the stolen data. While Hunt.io notified the CERT Philippines (CERT-PH) and the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW), the company declined to provide any more details of the national responses to the leak.

Related:Venezuelan Cartel's Malware Honcho Nabbed for ATM Jackpotting

However, Borges did say that, so far, the information has not appeared for sale on the Dark Web.

"We haven't seen the backups surface for sale or in a leak," he says. "We never opened the backups themselves."

Governments in the region need to scan their own networks and lock down their attack surface area, he says. Workers with too many privileges allow attackers with tools such as SeImpersonate to gain more access to assets on the network. Hunt.io also found that the migrant-worker portal exposed a number of risky ports, including SMB on 445 and WinRM on 5985 and 47001.

#10462. Technical Aspects of AI-Generated Video Assets for Web Design

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI-generated videos are becoming an important part of modern web design. Designers can now create animated backgrounds, product demonstrations, hero section videos, and visual storytelling elements without relying entirely on traditional video production. However, generating a visually appealing video is only one part of the process. To use AI-generated videos effectively on a website, developers and designers must also understand video formats, visual quality, file optimization, and website performance.

These technical factors directly influence how videos appear across devices, how quickly pages load, and how smoothly visitors interact with a website.

Video format selection is one of the first technical decisions when preparing AI-generated assets for the web. Different formats offer different levels of compression, compatibility, and visual quality.

For most websites, MP4 with H.264 remains a dependable default. WebM or AV1 can be offered as additional formats where appropriate.

Developers should also consider browser compatibility before selecting a format. Providing multiple sources allows browsers to choose a supported option.

AI-generated videos can sometimes contain visual inconsistencies, unnatural movements, distorted objects, or changes in lighting between frames. These issues become more noticeable when videos are displayed in large website sections.

Resolution is an important factor in maintaining visual quality. Common resolutions include:

However, higher resolution does not automatically mean better website performance or user experience. A 4K video may look impressive, but loading it unnecessarily can increase bandwidth consumption.

Frame rate also affects the viewing experience. Many website videos work well at 24 or 30 frames per second. Higher frame rates may be useful for fast-moving scenes, but they also increase the amount of visual data that needs to be processed.

Designers should review AI-generated footage before publishing it. Checking transitions, motion consistency, sharpness, and color accuracy helps prevent distracting visual problems.

Large video files can significantly increase website loading times. This is especially important for websites with video backgrounds, animated landing pages, and multiple visual sections.

Video optimization involves reducing file size without making the footage noticeably worse.

Some practical optimization techniques include:

Compression: Video compression reduces unnecessary data while preserving important visual details. Developers can use encoding tools such as FFmpeg to adjust bitrate, resolution, and codec settings.

Bitrate control: Bitrate determines how much data is used to represent each second of video. A higher bitrate generally preserves more detail but increases file size. Selecting an appropriate bitrate depends on the video's resolution, movement, and intended display size.

Trimming unnecessary footage: Website videos rarely need to be several minutes long. Removing unused sections helps reduce file size and keeps visual content focused.

Removing unnecessary audio: Background videos that do not require sound should be exported without an audio track. This reduces unnecessary data and supports a cleaner user experience.

Responsive video delivery: Websites should serve appropriately sized assets for different screen sizes. A smaller video may be sufficient for mobile users, while desktop visitors can receive a higher-resolution version.

These techniques help developers balance visual quality with efficient content delivery.

Even a well-optimized video can affect website performance if it is implemented incorrectly. Developers should consider how videos are loaded, displayed, and processed by browsers.

For example, automatically loading several large videos when a page opens can consume significant bandwidth. Instead, developers can use lazy loading strategies for videos that appear further down the page.

For background videos, the HTML video element offers several useful attributes:

Developers should also avoid autoplaying large videos unnecessarily. A static image can often provide a better experience on mobile devices or slower connections.

Performance testing tools such as Google Lighthouse and Chrome DevTools can help identify whether video assets are affecting loading speed, bandwidth usage, or rendering performance.

Technical optimization should not come at the expense of accessibility. Background videos should not distract users or make website content difficult to understand.

Developers should respect the prefers-reduced-motion media query, which allows users who prefer reduced animation to receive a less motion-intensive experience.

A suitable static background image can be displayed as an alternative.

Mobile compatibility is equally important. Smaller screens, limited data plans, and varying network conditions can make heavy video assets less practical. Testing videos on different devices and connection speeds helps identify potential problems before publication.

AI-generated video assets offer exciting possibilities for modern web design, but their successful implementation requires more than creative output. Choosing suitable video formats, maintaining consistent visual quality, compressing files, and considering website performance are all essential parts of the development process.

By combining thoughtful video production with responsive delivery, accessibility considerations, and performance testing, designers and developers can create engaging websites without compromising loading speed or usability. As AI video technology continues to evolve, understanding these technical fundamentals will remain valuable for building efficient and visually appealing web experiences.

Following the preview at the end of last month, Google is now bringing its latest Gemini 4 Carbon model to the Gemini app.

Officially, Google says “Argon remains the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work, while Carbon is built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence.” Examples include “complex, multi-step coding and debugging and open-ended scientific research and discovery.”

In the model picker, 4 Argon is for “Code & analysis” and 4 Carbon is for “Most complex work.” Notably, the Gemini app has removed 3.1 Pro with this launch.

Developers can assign Carbon to roles that demand the deepest reasoning, like architectural design, coordination, and auditing, while pairing it with faster, lighter models across parallel isolated workspaces and adversarial verifiers that test every change.

For legal, finance, and enterprise work, Carbon is said to bring “higher-precision knowledge work, artifact generation, and data analysis.” This includes how the model will follow “strict schemas and formatting to generate polished and precise spreadsheets, presentations, and reports.”

Existing benchmarks don’t adequately capture how agents reason natively over dense files with charts, images, blueprints, schematics, and tables, so we partnered with Artificial Analysis to launch the new Multimodal Knowledge Agents (MKA) benchmark. Carbon ranks #1 while using 3X fewer tokens than the next best model across 200 tasks that test a model’s multimodal performance in agentic workflows.

The introductory pricing for Carbon is $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens until November 30. Afterward, it will cost $4 per 1M input tokens and $20 per 1M output tokens.

#10454. More game developers are starting to use generative AI

The GDC Festival of Gaming’s latest annual industry survey shows an increase in AI usage among game developers.﻿

The GDC Festival of Gaming’s latest annual industry survey shows an increase in AI usage among game developers.﻿

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

More video game developers are using generative AI tools in their jobs compared to last year, according to the GDC Festival of Gaming’s latest annual industry survey. Forty percent of developers surveyed say they use it “as part of their job,” an increase from 36 percent in 2025. Usage was higher with game developers that work on free-to-play games at 58 percent and mobile-only studio workers at 70 percent.

The survey is being published as the game industry continues to reckon with generative AI tools. While many game developers, particularly indie developers, have spoken out strongly against the technology, AI is at the center of indie awards conversations in part because Big Walk developer House House “sparingly” used LLMs to assist with technical challenges in the “final stretch” of development. AI is also increasingly being used to reverse-engineer retro games. And in a post on Thursday, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma seemed to indicate that AI will be central to Xbox’s future, saying that “A small team will be able to build worlds that today demand hundreds of developers and hundreds of millions of dollars.”

Seventy three percent of the survey’s respondents said they used AI for research and brainstorming, while 62 percent used it for data analysis and summarization, and 56 percent for code generation and debugging. Twenty two percent of respondents used generative AI for concept art or visual ideation, and 8 percent used it for production art or final game assets.

The survey also included grim numbers about layoffs, with 34 percent of respondents saying they have been laid off sometime in the past two years.

#10453. Best AI Humanizer Tools Tested and Compared: 7 Options for Web Content

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

The best AI humanizer for web content is the one that changes how a draft reads without changing what it says. If you need a specific tone, Humanize Max gives you four styles and three lengths in one run. If you already work in QuillBot or Grammarly, their humanizers fit the account you have. GPTinf, Humanize AI and Undetectable AI put an AI check next to the rewrite, and Ahrefs gives you quick variants of a short passage.

To compare them on equal terms, we ran the same 103-word AI-written release note through each tool in November 2026. It contains a product name, two image formats, a settings path and the word "must", so it shows whether a tool keeps the details a reader acts on. We also checked every feature, limit and price on the vendor's own pages on the same day.

A humanizer earns its place only if its output needs fewer fixes than the draft you started with, and these six checks show whether a tool will do that for your content.

Humanize Max is a single-purpose humanizer: you paste an AI draft, upload a file or load the built-in sample, choose a style and a length, and get a rewritten version in a few seconds. The four styles are Academic, Casual, Creative and Formal, and the three lengths are Shorten, Standard and Expand, so you can turn a stiff feature description into casual blog copy and trim it in the same run.

The result highlights every phrase it changed, which makes it quick to check whether a product name or a settings path came through. If the rewrite doesn't land, Run it again produces a different version of the whole text. At the time of writing, it takes up to 2,000 words per run and works without an account.

Pricing: Plans and limits are still being finalized, so check the site for current terms.

Best for: Rewriting AI drafts of blog posts, product pages and emails into a specific tone.

QuillBot's AI Humanizer sits next to its paraphraser, grammar checker and AI detector, which makes it a natural pick if you already use QuillBot for rewording. Basic mode is free for up to 125 words per run, while Advanced mode, which rewrites more deeply, comes with Premium (the pricing page also lists three Advanced uses on the free plan). In our test, it asked us to create a free account before it showed the first result.

Premium removes the word limit and adds Freeze words, which keeps the terms you choose unchanged, along with tone insights, a history of past runs and a Chrome extension that humanizes text inside ChatGPT and Gemini.

Pricing: Basic mode is free. Premium is listed at $8.33 a month, billed annually.

Best for: Quick fixes to a paragraph or two for writers who already use QuillBot.

GPTinf is a writing toolkit built around its humanizer, with an AI detector, plagiarism checker, grammar checker, paraphraser and readability checker on the same site. The humanizer has two modes, Standard and Academic, and takes pasted text or a PDF, Word or plain-text file. File-to-File mode returns the humanized document in its original format, so a long brief keeps its layout.

Custom Style lets you paste 150 to 1,200 words of your own writing, and later runs are shaped to match it, with no account needed. After each run, an AI-likelihood estimate appears under the output, so you can see whether a draft needs another pass. Treat that number as a probability, not proof of who wrote the text.

Pricing: A free plan is available. Paid plans start at $9.99 a month for Lite (5,000 words), with Pro at $24.99 and Unlimited at $59.99.

Best for: Freelancers and content teams that want to rewrite and check drafts without switching tools.

Grammarly's AI Humanizer comes in two layers. The tool on its web page is free, works without an account and offers basic humanization of pasted text or an uploaded document. A free Grammarly account adds the Humanizer agent, with four preset styles, a custom voice built from a writing sample, and support for English, Spanish, French, German, Portuguese and Italian.

Grammarly says the humanizer focuses on clarity and readability rather than on AI detectors, which matches how most web teams use these tools. If you need to show how a piece was written, Grammarly Authorship shows which parts came from AI, which came from online sources and which you wrote yourself. The basic tool's word counter allows up to 1,500 words per run.

Pricing: The basic humanizer is free. Grammarly Pro is listed at $12 on the plans page, which doesn't state the billing period.

Best for: Teams that already write in Grammarly and want one voice across documents.

Humanize AI is built for people who want to tune the output. Without an account you get the Free tone, a Rewrite level slider with three stops (Quality, Balanced and Max) and Custom style, which learns your voice from 150 to 1,200 words of samples. A free account opens eight more modes, including Formal, Informal, Academic, Expand and Shorten, and on desktop a Writing level menu sets how plain or dense the result reads.

View changes highlights every edit, and File-to-File accepts PDF, DOCX, TXT and MD documents and returns them in the same format. Paid plans also include a public API that supports the same styles and rewrite levels as the web app, so a developer can add a humanizing step to a CMS or publishing pipeline.

Pricing: Paid plans start at $9.99 a month for Lite (10,000 words), with Standard at $19.99 and Unlimited at $59.99. Yearly billing lowers the monthly price.

Best for: Teams that need precise tone control or want to humanize text through an API.

Undetectable AI keeps its humanizer simple: one text box, one button and no style or length settings. Its free allowance works differently from the others, with 1,000 words in total before you need an account and another 1,000 once you create a free one.

Under the output, a Check for AI button runs a detection check on the result, and the same site has a separate AI detector and plagiarism checker. Its FAQ says pasted text isn't published or shared but doesn't say whether it's stored, so keep confidential details out of the drafts you run through it.

Pricing: Paid plans start at $9.99 a month for Lite (5,000 words), with Pro at $25 (25,000 words) and Unlimited at $59 (1,000,000 words). Yearly billing lowers the monthly price.

Best for: Trying a humanizer on a full-length draft before you commit to an account.

Ahrefs, best known for its SEO platform, offers a free AI Text Humanizer among its writing tools. You paste up to 2,048 characters, choose one, three or five variants, and pick the version that reads best. It ran without an account in our test.

Variants are the useful part. For a hero headline, a meta description or a product blurb, comparing three rewrites side by side is faster than prompting a chatbot three times, and you can export all results as a text file. The character limit, which fits a few short paragraphs, rules it out for full articles.

Best for: Short marketing copy where you want several options to choose from.

The best AI humanizer tool for a documentation team isn't the one a growth marketer needs, so match the tool to the content in front of you.

There isn't one winner, because these tools solve different problems. The quickest way to decide is to run a paragraph from your own work, ideally one with a product name, a number and an instruction, through two or three of the tools above, and keep the one whose output you'd publish with the fewest fixes.

Google's guidance on using generative AI content is about value rather than the tool: mass-producing pages that add nothing for readers can count as scaled content abuse. A humanizer changes phrasing, not usefulness, so the same rules apply. Google also recommends fact-checking AI-generated titles, meta descriptions and image alt text before you publish.

The best humanizer for your team is the one whose controls match your content: tone presets for blog posts, variants for short copy, change highlighting for docs and a custom voice for marketing. Run one of your own paragraphs through two or three tools from this list, then read every highlighted change, especially names, numbers and words like "must", before anything goes live.

#10451. Nintendo Switch 2 emulation on Android already has The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake up and running

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake now runs surprisingly well on phones after just a week of additional emulator development.

Legend of Zelda fans all over the world have been marveling at the Ocarina of Time remake’s visuals and enhanced gameplay systems on the Nintendo Switch 2, but the Android emulator scene has been busy marveling over something just a little bit different. One Redditor got the latest Zelda game running on Banana Native, a free emulator that’s available right now on GitHub.

Ocarina of Time remake performance has now reached a major milestone into the 30 FPS territory with frame gen, which means the game is actually running at around 15 FPS, but then scaled and interpolated using AI frame generation to appear like 30 FPS. Banana Native isn’t a traditional emulator, as it doesn’t emulate hardware. Rather, it uses the game’s own ARM64 code to run on the phone’s CPU. The Switch 2 is powered by a mobile Nvidia chip, after all.

The user is running the Ocarina of Time remake on a Poco F7 Ultra, which sports a two-generation-old Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite (Gen 4) processor. The latest phones that are coming out, like the Redmagic 12 Pro, run a 6th-gen Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme chip, so performance could be a lot better on a newer phone. Apps like Banana Native require specific driver support for each phone to run, and as I pointed out in my Redmagic 12 Pro review, platforms like Droid Deck and Game Native don’t yet have proper drivers for the newest chips.

9to5Google’s Damien Wilde recently reviewed Droid Deck, another native-type emulator that lets you legally play Steam games you own on your phone by just signing into your Steam account. It works extremely well on lots of Android phones and helps showcase just how far Android emulation has come this year.
